📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as we barrel towards December, money is top of mind for a lot of moms. And, really, that makes sense any year: the holidays are expensive. As moms, we’re always doing the math in our heads: how much we can afford, how much we need to cut, how much is going out vs. how much is coming in. And this year, a lot of moms are finding that the math just ain’t mathing. That theme kept surfacing in this week’s roundup of anonymous confessions.

One mom wants a divorce but says that, in this economy, it isn’t possible. Another admits that, financially, she regrets having her third child. One mom got laid off and one mom is tired of working her ass off yet always feeling broke, and one mom, in her own words, just wants to be left alone with a lot of money.

The cost of everything is dictating a lot right now, and moms are really feeling that.

Industry observers note that then there are the other confessions that revealed up this week, the kind that bubble up every week. Worries about being a good parent. Health concerns. Perimenopause (always perimenopause!). Little wins that moms need to share with someone.

So, here are this week’s confessions, shared anonymously by moms yelling into the void about everything from money to marriage.

Scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram. And to browse past Confessions, take a look here.

Did You Know You Have a Birth Month Winter Bird? Here's All 12 and Their Special Meanings

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seasons are shifting, which means our feathered friends are about to embark upon a changing of the guard...
  • It has been revealed that it's not a silly question, by any means.
  • According to recent reports, with that in mind, then, what if every month had its own winter bird to call its own?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seasons are shifting, which means our feathered friends are about to embark upon a changing of the guard... so which is your birth month winter bird, you ask?

It has been revealed that it's not a silly question, by any means. After all, some birds migrate south for winter, some arrive from further north, and year-round residents shift their habits. And, from the brilliant red cardinal perched against a snowy backdrop to the tiny dark-eyed junco hopping beneath a bird feeder, these seasonal visitors have plenty of personality.

According to recent reports, with that in mind, then, what if every month had its own winter bird to call its own? What might it reveal about the people born under its wings?

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a classic birth month bird, not to mention the birth month owl and birth month bird of prey, but what might the unique traits that make each winter bird so wonderful say about our own personalities?

According to recent reports, some are bold and charismatic, others are quiet and contemplative, and a few are wonderfully independent. All, though, are beautiful in their own special way, and so much fun to watch as they go about their business over the colder months.

In a recent development, with that in mind, then, I've paired 12 fascinating winter birds with the personality traits commonly associated with each birth month, along with a few easy ways you can make your garden a more welcoming place for them. Time to grab yourself a motion-activated wildlife camera with night vision, like the GardePro on Amazon, then, and start reading...

And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

According to recent reports, if you're born in January, you're likely to be headstrong, disciplined and hardworking (all of which are, natural leadership qualities, just in case you fancied informing your boss). Naturally, then, your birth month winter bird is a wonderful reflection of that determination: the snow bunting.

These beautiful little birds are highly social during winter, often gathering in flocks to forage for seeds in open fields and along shorelines, while their ability to thrive in bitterly cold conditions is rather impressive for such a small bird.

In a recent development, like January babies, basically, they don't shy away from a challenge; they meet it head-on! To help them do this, be sure to leave native grasses and seed-producing plants standing where possible, rather than tidying every corner of your garden.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most iconic birds in the world, the striking snowy owl has brilliant white plumage, piercing yellow eyes and an unmistakable presence. They spend much of the year in the Arctic, but some travel south during winter, occasionally appearing in northern parts of the United States (although they tend to favour wide-open landscapes, including coastal dunes, fields and other exposed areas where they can hunt).

According to recent reports, often solitary hunters, February's birth month winter bird gets by on its own instincts and remarkable ability to spot prey from a distance. It's also wonderfully adapted to its harsh environment, making it a fitting symbol of independence, deep-thinking, and inner strength.

To help snowy owls out over the colder months, avoid using rodenticides that can poison birds of prey, turn your garden into an owl hangout (it only takes five plants), and always give any owl you encounter plenty of space.

Sources indicate that march babies are often associated with introspection, creativity, compassion and a thoughtful nature. It makes a whole lot of sense, then, that their birth month winter bird is the dark-eyed junco, a small but charming visitor that brings plenty of life to colder gardens.

Sometimes nicknamed the snowbird, dark-eyed juncos tend to spend much of their time quietly hopping around on the ground, searching for fallen seeds beneath trees and feeders. As such, they're a lovely match for March personalities: observant, gentle and happy to enjoy the quieter things in life.

Sources indicate that if you fancy seeing more in your garden, remember that juncos are particularly fond of feeding on the ground, so provide a sheltered feeding area with small seeds. Leaving native grasses and seed heads standing also gives them more natural foraging opportunities.

Shop Junco Bird Feeding Essentials:.

Industry observers note that if you're an April baby, you're thought to be charismatic, energetic, straightforward and naturally confident. As such, there's perhaps no better bird to represent you than the unmistakable blue jay.

With its brilliant blue plumage, distinctive crest and loud calls, the blue jay certainly knows how to make itself noticed. These intelligent members of the crow family have bold personalities that often make them one of the most entertaining birds to watch, in fact.

Blue jays are also clever problem-solvers, not to mention never afraid to make their presence known. Plant native oak trees and other nut-producing species to provide natural food and shelter to help them out, and remember that they also enjoy unsalted peanuts , so you can occasionally offer some in a suitable feeder.

According to recent reports, I know, I know; a wild turkey might not feel like the most glamorous birth month winter bird, but hear me out! May personalities are often described as sociable, talented, loyal and strong-willed. And wild turkeys? Why, they're highly social, often gathering in flocks during winter as they search for food, not to mention putting on some impressive courtship displays.

Recent findings suggest that they're also resourceful foragers, searching through woodland floors for seeds, nuts, berries and insects. During colder months, they can be spotted scratching through leaf litter and searching beneath trees for whatever food they can find. To help yours out, then, take care to leave natural cover in place where possible, and avoid using pesticides that reduce the insects and other natural food sources they rely on.

Known for its melancholy-sounding coo, the gentle mourning dove is a familiar sight across much of the United States, often seen perched on telephone wires, fences and tree branches, or quietly searching the ground for seeds.

They're also known for their strong pair bonds, with partners often working together to raise their young, so it's easy to see why this bird suits June babies (especially as they tend to be such romantic dreamers). It's a birth month winter bird that perfectly aligns with all of that sensitivity and imagination.

Remember, mourning doves enjoy feeding on the ground, so provide a clean feeding area with something like sunflower hearts if you want to see them in your garden. Plant some native seed-producing plants and shrubs, too, to help provide natural food and shelter.

In a recent development, july babies are adventurous free spirits known for their cheerful and (ahem) slightly slightly eccentric personalities, not to mention their strong protective streaks when it comes to family. It was inevitable, then, that the snow goose would prove their birth month winter bird.

Known for their impressive journeys between breeding and wintering grounds, snow geese are often spotted travelling in enormous flocks that fill the sky with their distinctive calls. They are also strongly connected to family life; young birds travel with their parents, and family groups can remain together during migration and winter.

In a recent development, if you want to help your feathery soulmate out, remember that snow geese depend on healthy wetlands, grasslands and agricultural landscapes during migration and winter. Supporting wetland conservation and protecting natural resting and feeding areas, then, is one of the best ways to keeo them thriving.

It makes so much sense that August babies get the delightful red-breasted nuthatch as their birth month winter bird, as it sums up all their best qualities perfectly. Yes, this little bird might be small, but it certainly doesn't lack confidence. One of its most entertaining habits is climbing headfirst down tree trunks, something it does with remarkable ease as it searches for insects and seeds hidden in the bark.

During autumn and winter, red-breasted nuthatches also collect and store conifer seeds, helping ensure they have food available when conditions become more challenging. They're hardworking, resourceful and rather determined, making them a lovely match for August birthdays.

Sources indicate that to help them out, try to plant native trees such as pine, spruce and fir where appropriate for your region. You can also offer sunflower seeds, peanuts or suet in a clean feeder, particularly during colder weather.

Intelligent, spiritual, organized and analytical, September babies tend to be more successful in life (genuinely; look it up!) and thus are represented by the pine siskin.

According to recent reports, these small finches might be easy to overlook at first, but they're fascinating little birds. They are adaptable, clever, and brimming with plenty of resourcefulness, though, which is why you often seen clinging to the tips of pine branches and even hanging upside down as they extract seeds from cones.

According to recent reports, sure, they're rather unpredictable visitors, as their movements depend heavily on food availability; this means that some gardens might welcome large flocks one winter and see very few the next. To keep them flocking, grow native conifers and other seed-producing plants to provide natural food, as well as nyjer (thistle) seed and sunflower hearts in finch feeders.

Industry observers note that as an October baby myself, I'm more than happy to see this charming wanderer as my birth month winter bird! Especially as, with its striking yellow, black and white plumage and enormous pale bill, this chunky finch is one of North America's most distinctive birds.

Evening grosbeaks are adventurous travellers, sometimes moving considerable distances in search of food during autumn and winter. They're also wonderfully sociable, often gathering in groups around food sources and making quite an impression when they arrive at a backyard feeder.

For October birthdays, they're a lovely symbol of persistence, confidence and a little good fortune. After all, spotting one can feel like winning a small birdwatching lottery (although you can boost your chances with a handful of black-oil sunflower seeds, which can be offered in a sturdy platform feeder).

Empathetic, generous, brave and deeply determined, November-born souls are represented by one of North America's most magnificent waterbirds: the trumpeter swan.

These enormous white swans are impressive in every sense, with long necks, powerful wings and a distinctive black bill. They are known for their strong pair bonds and devoted parenting, and their family groups can be particularly striking to see gliding across a winter lake. In fact, it's their loyalty, protective instincts and graceful strength that make them a beautiful match for November birthdays.

These aren't traditional garden birds, so you can help them by protecting local wetlands, ponds and freshwater habitats, and always taking care to avoid disturbing swans when they're resting or feeding.

It has been revealed that generous, patriotic, optimistic and willing to take a few risks? Yeah, obviously the birth month winter bird for December is the cardinal!

Recent findings suggest that known for their strong pair bonds and the way they communicate through a variety of musical calls, their cheerful appearance against bare branches and snowy gardens has led to them becoming something not unlike a symbol of hope during the festive season. In fact, many believe that if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st, you're owed 12 months of love, optimism, and luck for the year ahead.

If you want to help yours out, plant native berry-producing shrubs such as winterberry, serviceberry and dogwood to make your garden a one-stop destination for food, shelter, and nesting opportunities.

Whether you believe in the concept of a birth month winter bird or not, there's no denying that they serve as a lovely reminder of just how much wildlife is around us, even during the coldest months of the year.

In a recent development, and perhaps the best part is that you don't have to wait for your own birth month to enjoy these feathered visitors. By planting native trees and shrubs, leaving seed heads standing, providing clean water and maintaining safe feeding areas, you can help make your garden a welcoming winter refuge for your feathered friends throughout the year.

Sources indicate that give it a go, I say! You'll do your bit for local wildlife and you might even discover a new favorite feathered friend along the way...

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

Industry observers note that âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â.

Mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own vital role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

In a recent development, different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

In a recent development, that Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

According to recent reports, during the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â.

It is a sweet story, but it also demonstrates why understanding each dog's personality matters.

Industry observers note that hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â.

Sources indicate that camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

It has been revealed that three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

It has been revealed that two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her latest home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

Industry observers note that âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â states Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â.

In a recent development, some dogs find their people swiftly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:.

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â.

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

It has been revealed that at Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Maybe that is what makes them lucky.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

In a recent development, and that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

And every morning, people arrive.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

There are a number of reasons cats tend to be picky when it comes to mealtime. Depending on your feline, you may be dealing with one or all of these difficult instincts and sensitivities.

Recent findings suggest that to start, cats have a very sensitive sense of smell. Even quality food can be turned down if the aroma is too unfamiliar. Cats are also very finicky about textures. They tend to develop very specific preferences about how foods should feel in their mouth. This makes it both hard to introduce new foods and to keep your cat from getting bored with the very specific foods they like.

Many cats exhibit neophobiaâa fear of new things. This doesnât just apply to new people, places, and toys, either. Cats evolved to be naturally wary of new food items and prey. This is likely because their ancestors lived in the desert where many little creatures are deadlier than their size might indicate. While modern cat food isnât likely to be venomous, your cat's instincts still tell them to beware anything they havenât eaten before.

Every Japanese Maple Needs Some TLC Before Winter – 6 Easy Tasks to Protect Your Prized Tree

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage.
  • It has been revealed that japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage.
  • So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

It has been revealed that japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

So you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

Don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

According to recent reports, however, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

Tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

Don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

It has been revealed that in these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

If your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

According to recent reports, would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces newly introduced growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

Industry observers note that in spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

You’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Sources indicate that trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

Recent findings suggest that this means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

Latest Update: I Travel With A Kid Who Has Severe Allergies. Here Are The Things I Never Thought To Worry About

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that everyday things can send us to the hospital.
  • Recent findings suggest that my son has severe allergies, asthma, and celiac disease, so everyday things can sometimes send us to the hospital.
  • Sources indicate that with the colder weather settling in and holiday travel approaching, I knew it was time to take a closer look at what families like mine should be considering before hitting the road or boarding a plane.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that everyday things can send us to the hospital. Now I’m prepared and am sharing the wealth.

Recent findings suggest that my son has severe allergies, asthma, and celiac disease, so everyday things can sometimes send us to the hospital. And traveling adds another layer of uncertainty. A hotel room that looks clean could be holding fragrances that trigger respiratory symptoms. The swimming pool down the hall could pose problemsThat gluten-free item on the menu during our family night out could be cross-contaminated. As a parent, I’ve learned that keeping my son safe means thinking beyond the obvious risks.

Sources indicate that with the colder weather settling in and holiday travel approaching, I knew it was time to take a closer look at what families like mine should be considering before hitting the road or boarding a plane. So, I chatted with experts Dr. Sarah Beebe, a travel advisor and autism travel professional based in Lewes, Delaware, and Dr. Tracy Tyson, a pediatrician with 20 years experience in urgent care, who helped me identify the less obvious triggers families might encounter while traveling—and how to better prepare for them.

Through the colder months and when planning trips, I’d always assumed that keeping my son’s inhaler on hand was enough. But a recent hospital stay made me realize his asthma is far more severe than we’d understood, and that I needed to take a more proactive approach to managing it.

In a recent development, I researched all of the common triggers, such as dust, pet dander, pollen, smoke and weather changes. After chatting with Dr. Tyson and Dr. Beebe, I learned of the lesser-known hazards that can lurk in the places we stay and the ways we travel.

“A lot of high-end hotels have a signature scent in the lobby and common areas, and most people find it lovely, but for a kid with asthma or sensory sensitivities, it can be a lot,” Beebe told me. No parent can demand these scents be removed, of course. But we can be aware and prepare accordingly.

On top of fragrances, “detergents in bedding and cleaning supplies will do it, too,” Tyson remarked. What can families do? Request fragrance-free bedding, or bring their own.

When planning family trips, we always look for a place with a pool. Swimming is one of our favorite pastimes, and I never considered that it might be contributing to my kids’ symptoms. But thinking back, my son often develops a runny nose and needs to lie down after a swim.

Industry observers note that “The heavy chlorine smell is actually chloramines sitting in the air over a pool that isn't well ventilated, and it's a real irritant,” Beebe explained. She once treated a child who came into the emergency room she was working in after swimming multiple days in a hotel pool. “He began having a cough and shortness of breath. He came to the ER in significant distress because the high levels of chlorine in the pool triggered a more severe asthma exacerbation and he didn’t have any rescue medications with him,” she mentioned. Luckily, there was an emergency room nearby.

“Thunderstorms can break up pollen and trigger asthma,” Tyson explained. When traveling through the rainy season, keep windows closed and stay indoors when storms approach. But don’t assume the risk disappears as soon as the skies clear; thunderstorm-related asthma can occur after the storm. If you do venture outside, have your child rinse off and change clothes when you return to your lodging, to help remove pollen from the skin and hair.

Sources indicate that planning a New Year’s trip with the kids? Keep in mind that fireworks can pose a double challenge for autistic kids with asthma. “Fireworks smoke blows right over the crowd depending on the wind,” Beebe shared, and the noise and crowds can add another layer of sensory overwhelm. Her advice? Find a viewing spot farther from the launch site and upwind of the smoke, if possible. Your child can enjoy the show without being right in the middle of it.

Industry observers note that along with his many allergies, my son has severe celiac disease. When his symptoms first appeared, doctors were concerned enough that they thought his presentation resembled leukemia. He was spiking fevers, developing spots on his skin, struggling with abdominal challenges and shortness of breath. My son would wake up fine, then spike a fever by noon and be on the couch until dinner—for days and days until we figured it out.

Now, when he’s exposed to gluten, he can vomit profusely. And for him, the risk isn’t limited to taking a bite of food containing gluten. Cross-contact –when gluten transfers from contaminated surfaces or other foods — can be a problem, too.

And so I chatted with Tyson and Beebe about what celiac triggers to look for when not at home.

“Welcome treats, lounge snacks, the chocolate on the pillow. None of it gets the care a restaurant meal does,” Beebe mentioned. “And half the time it isn't gluten-free, never mind certified.” If your child is young, there’s a chance they may snag one or more of these things when your back is turned, so we have to think ahead. “When I plan a trip, I have the allergy flagged on the reservation so the extras get caught too, not just the dining rooms,” Beebe added.

Recent findings suggest that paper straws had never crossed my mind as a potential source of gluten exposure. I can think of more than one time I’ve bought my son a drink without giving the straw a second thought. “A lot of them use a wheat-based binder to hold the straw together,” Beebe remarked. “So even the eco-friendly straw can be a problem.” Keeping a few reusable or plastic straws on hand–or bringing your own drinks—can offer a simple alternative.

Traveling in different countries is ever harder, since the warnings aren’t as clear and there is often unintended gluten exposure, Tyson told me. “This is the one families never see coming, and it's the one I warn them about,” Beebe said. “You’re fine early in the trip, but after days of eating where you can't control the kitchen, the little exposures stack up, and the worst reaction tends to hit at the very end.”.

Industry observers note that one thing Tyson pointed out that I hadn’t considered is how the stress of travel can complicate celiac disease management. Even without a known gluten exposure, the disruption of routines can affect how your child feels. “During travel people often allow little amounts of gluten which combined with above can cause a flare,” she stated.

Industry observers note that so, what can families do to help with all of this? Well, proposal travel around places known as safe havens for people with celiac disease. Disney has an entire department devoted to complex allergies, Beebe shared. “And you can call ahead of time, so they're prepared for your kids with severe and complex needs before you ever arrive.”.

Learning about these lesser known triggers has given me something I didn’t have before: a greater sense of control. Instead of approaching travel with the anxiety and dread that can come with managing my kids’ needs away from home, I feel more equipped to protect him–and more excited about the adventures ahead.

This holiday season, as we move from one place to the next, we’ll be better prepared for what we might encounter along the way. And if you’re coparenting like I am, there’s another kind of peace that comes with this knowledge: knowing you can share what you’ve learned with the people caring for your children, so they can help keep them safe, too. We may not be able to anticipate every trigger, but we can make it easier for our kids to explore the world with a little less risk–and a lot less worry.

Industry observers note that so just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. It has been revealed that ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

Of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

It has been revealed that this low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

Industry observers note that you can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that when you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

According to recent reports, A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

Think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

It has been revealed that then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

This is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

Here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

In a recent development, you aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially vital if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

Recent findings suggest that A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

The bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the upcoming, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

If you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

This lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

Sources indicate that if you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.

Fuller looking lashes with zero transfer? Yes please.

According to recent reports, as a fair-skinned, dark-haired lady of Scottish descent, I haven’t always appreciated my very hairy ancestry (like when my little brother told me I have arms hairier than a man’s). But along with the body hair gene comes one I’m thankful for: I’ve always had long eyelashes. When I’m shopping for mascaras, I gravitate toward volumizing formulas that make my lashes look full from root to tip. And as I get older and the skin around my eyes creases and (sob) sags in latest ways, I also need mascaras that won’t transfer and leave dark smudges on my top and bottom lids.

When KJH — a brand founded by celebrity MUA Katie Jane Hughes — offered to send me their new Microscara, I was intrigued. I love a tubing mascara because they’re pretty darn transfer proof (and the easy removal is so nice), but I wasn’t sure how volumizing a tubing formula could really be. And that teensy wand? I dunno... But let me tell you, after wearing it for months, this is the stuff right here.

KJH describes the Microscara as a smudge-proof tubing mascara that “delivers instant volume and length that lasts.” The differentiator here is the micro wand designed to grab and coat even the smallest, hardest-to-reach lashes for a “full-lash finish that won’t budge.”.

The Microscara’s significant selling point is the small wand. It’s about half the length of your typical mascara wand, and it is very slim at the tapered end. The bristles feel like a typical volumizing wand (more, thinner bristles instead of the spiky plastic kind). And because the brush is so slim, the tube is too — it’s extremely lightweight and lovely to travel with.

Mascara is always the last step in my makeup routine (even after setting spray, because I don’t want to wet my mascara and encourage smudging). With any mascara, I like to hold the brush right at the root of my lashes, wiggle it back and forth so the bristles can grab on, and then move the wand up to coat each lash. My best tip is to also hold the wand behind your lashes to coat the tops and catch the curly tips of each eyelash. You’ll be shocked how much visual length this adds to your lashes overall.

My whole routine works so much better with the Microscara because of its slim brush. I’m not accidentally getting mascara on my lids, and I can wiggle the brush into the corners of my eyes and coat even the smallest lashes.

A little side-by-side comparison of my bare lashes and the KJH Microscara’s handiwork.

Industry observers note that OK, one of my favorite things about using the KJH Microscara is that, because I can get so close to my lash line with the little brush, it basically looks like I’m wearing eyeliner and can skip that step completely. My lash line itself just looks fuller. C’est magnifique.

Recent findings suggest that with other tubing formulas, I feel like they add length but my lashes end up looking a little sparse, and that is simply not the case here. I can see a genuine difference in the look of both the volume and length of my lashes when I use the product. I am someone who gets mascara smudges with pretty much any formula (even the waterproof ones), but this product has only ever given me a smudge once, and I think it was my fault, TBH.

Much like foundations, mascaras can be pretty personal. What works like a dream for one person could be a disaster on someone else. But I think if you’re in the market for a mascara that adds volume and is easy to remove, you won’t be disappointed by the Microscara.

I haven’t reached for any other mascara since I cracked the lid on this one.

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Sources indicate that since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

According to recent reports, if you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an crucial source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

Industry observers note that I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

Even if you’re not comfortable taking medication, there are other treatment options out there.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re a parent, it’s sometimes hard to tell what is a normal amount of tired and what’s an unhealthy level of exhaustion. Aren’t we all at least a little bit tired all the time? So when should you talk to your doctor about sleep challenges? But if you’ve been struggling night after night to fall asleep, you can’t seem to stay asleep, or you never feel well-rested in the mornings, it might be a sign that your sleep needs a little TLC. And yes, even if you’re hesitant to take medications to help you fall and stay asleep, there are actually other treatment options you can try.

Scary Mommy spoke with Dr. Jessica Meers, board-certified sleep psychologist and founder of Rhythm Wellness Sleep Solutions, to find out where you should turn for insomnia help first — and what treatment options even exist.

When does “I’m struggling to fall asleep lately” become “I should really see my doctor about this”?

In a recent development, “If it feels like a problem to you, it’s worth having a conversation about,” claims Meers. Whether you’re overly tired during the daytime, feel like you can’t sleep long or well enough, or just unhappy with your sleep in one way or another, that’s reason enough to ask for help, she says.

And how do you know if you really have insomnia? Is there a line where sleep troubles become clinical?

It has been revealed that “Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking up too early, or just having really poor, unrefreshing sleep. There are no guidelines on how long it takes you to fall asleep or how long you’re awake in the middle of the night, but you have to be unhappy with it at least three times a week for at least three months for it to meet full criteria for chronic insomnia,” Meers explains.

According to recent reports, if you’ve noticed your husband starts snoring within seconds of his head hitting the pillow, you’re not alone. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which experts have chalked up to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the bulk of the mental load in the family.

“One of the biggest reasons we think for this is that as women, we cycle through our monthly menstrual cycle, and the dynamics and the changing of those hormones set us up to have more disrupted and more fragmented sleep at certain times of the cycle versus other times,” notes Meers.

Industry observers note that “Also, we have a lot of role strain as women. We carry a lot of caretaking activities and responsibilities, especially in women who are in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, who are trying to take care of everyone and have a career and be productive and make sure that we’re taking care of our kids the way we value or give them the life we want them to live. Stress directly impacts insomnia and our ability to sleep. So it really becomes this negative feedback cycle.”.

You could definitely start by scheduling an appointment with your primary care doctor, if you have one. However, surveys show the average doctor only receives about 2.5 hours of education on sleep during medical school. Depending on your concerns and potential causes of your sleeplessness, they might refer you to a sleep medicine physician, a neurologist, a psychiatrist, or a sleep psychologist.

You may have never heard of sleep psychologists like Meers before, but they are specifically trained in the dynamics of sleep and sussing out underlying medical causes of insomnia (like sleep apnea) versus behavioral causes.

“I talk to a lot of primary care physicians. A lot of times they feel constrained to just give medications, nor do they have the time to really assess what’s going on because they have just so much to do in such a short amount of time,” Meers notes. “So if you have the ability to see a sleep specialist like me who's a psychologist, I recommend starting there. And then if this is a medical issue, we are really good at determining that and then sending you along to the right treatment provider.”.

Sources indicate that sleep psychologists are a great resource if you want to try other treatment options before turning to medication. The American Psychological Association has a psychologist finder where you can enter your zip code and search specifically for sleep psychologists in your area. You could also check with your insurance provider or ask your PCP if they know of any sleep psychologists near you.

According to recent reports, many people start trying to fix their sleep with supplements like melatonin or magnesium. They might turn to their primary care doctor next and either try a medication and love the results, or feel a little stuck because they don’t want meds, but there’s not much else being offered.

In a recent development, if there is an underlying medical cause for your sleeplessness, like restless legs syndrome or sleep apnea, treating that condition should alleviate the insomnia. For everyone else, Meers notes medication can be a wonderful tool, but treatment should start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I.

“That’s what the research indicates is most effective. So when somebody comes to me, I’m like, ‘I want you to do what’s going to be most effective for you.’ And so my goal is to start with cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia.”.

CBT-I is very different from cognitive behavioral therapy to treat something like anxiety or depression. It helps bridge the connection between your biology and your psychology, Meers indicates.

Industry observers note that “The way that cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia works is that we are using our understanding of the biology of sleep to get your behaviors in line with your biology. We are not just focusing on sleep timing, but also how your body has learned to sleep poorly and how do we unlearn that.”.

CBT-I is actually a pretty short treatment, compared to most intends in the field of psychology — an average of just four to eight sessions, indicates Meers.

According to recent reports, “It’s very skills-based, meaning I’m teaching a lot of skills in the first four sessions, and then for the next few sessions, we’re just tracking our progress and seeing how things are working. You are changing a lot of your habits, and you’re changing those habits in the service of retraining your body and your mind to associate the bed with sleep. I’m literally telling people to get out of bed, here’s what you do when you get out of bed, here’s what to think about, and then here’s when you get into bed, here’s your sleep schedule for the next week.”.

Industry observers note that the moral of the story is that you shouldn’t wait to tell someone — your PCP, a sleep psychologist, your usual therapist — about your sleep struggles. Whether you want to try CBT-I, find a medication that works for you, or investigate a possible issue like sleep apnea, there is help out there for sleeplessness.

For starters, they’re more common than you’d think.

After having my second baby, my body was a mess: hair falling out, boobs engorged — the works. So when I peed a little when I sneezed, it didn’t seem like a big deal. Until it happened again. And again. Eventually, I managed to sneeze, cough, and laugh without feeling some bladder leakage, but it took a few months for my body to get the memo.

In a recent development, these days, everyone talks about their pelvic floor: what it is, how to strengthen it, how having a baby can wreck it. But bladder leakage — which can be related to that all-important pelvic floor and the stress it undergoes during pregnancy and labor — tends to fly under the radar. No one wants to talk about it, maybe because there’s still a stigma attached to bathroom issues. Even though I’ve discussed every other postpartum thing under the sun (padsicles! Peri bottles! Nipple shields!) with my friends, urinary incontinence has never entered the chat.

But fortunately, Poise is ready to. The brand’s variety of bladder-leakage pads makes it easy to find exactly what you want, be it feels-like-you’re-wearing-nothing protection or a pad that keeps you dry all day. With that, here’s everything I wish someone had warned me about ahead of time.

Bladder leakage might not come up a lot (or at all) in the group chat, but a lot of women experience it. In fact, a large scientific review found that one in three women experiences bladder leakage between six weeks and a year after giving birth — whether it’s their first child or their third. So you’re probably not the only mom at the baby music class who’s dealing with the occasional accident. It only seems like a rarity because no one talks about it, when really it’s a legitimate and very normal part of recovering from birth. And that’s a disservice, because when people aren’t comfortable talking about issues like this, then the solutions don’t receive attention, either.

So you have some accidental leakage and want to give your old period pads a shot. While your average maxi-pad might do the trick if your leak is small, do you really want to risk an impromptu pants change while you’re out and about with your baby? If not, then you might need to consider more protection with a pad that’s actually designed for bladder leaks, like Poise's Pads for Bladder Leaks.

It has been revealed that poise’s pads promptly absorb wetness and trap odor so that no one but you knows what you're dealing with, and they come with layers that wick moisture and keep you feeling dry. On top of up to 12 hours of protection, they stay 25 times drier than the leading period pad. Plus, Poise Bladder Leak Pads have a thoughtful, contoured design that prevents bunching — so you can wear them under leggings and no one will know the difference.

A pad that can handle bladder leakage might sound huge, bulky, and like a wedgie waiting to happen. After all, super-thick pads can get tricky when you’re exercising, might need adjustment when you’re out and about, or can just be flat-out be annoying to wear.

But you don’t actually have to sacrifice comfort for protection. Poise Ultra Thin Pads for Bladder Leaks with Wings can handle moderate bladder leaks, absorbing wetness and neutralizing odors so you feel (and smell) fresh all day. They have layers that have been specifically designed to handle more wetness and help you stay dry, so you can focus on more crucial things, like enjoying postpartum life!

Sources indicate that bladder leaks after baby make a lot of sense, considering the many ways in which pushing a kid out can affect with your body. But (sorry in advance!) they can also occur at other times in your life, too — like during the menopause transition. It's not that perimenopause itself leads to bladder leakage, but natural changes in your body during this time, such as weight gain and anxiety, can contribute to it, according to one study.

Sources indicate that and, as you can imagine when you have a baby bouncing around on top of your bladder (and frequently kicking it), leakage can also happen during pregnancy itself — not just after delivery. It’s actually more common than it is postpartum: Roughly four in 10 women experience bladder leakage during pregnancy, according to one analysis.

This is all to say: Bladder leaks are a normal part of life, whether you’re having a baby, recently gave birth, or are just getting older. And when that happens, it’s a relief to have protection that you can count on — and actually feel confident and comfortable wearing. After all, there are a lot of things to worry about when you become a mom; having to swap out your underwear shouldn’t be one of them.

In a recent development, some kittens steal your heart with their big eyes. Others win you over with their playful antics. And then there's Gelato, a tiny kitten who needed a wheelchair and ended up getting one made from Hot Wheels cars. Yes, really. Human ingenuity and humane creativity to the rescue!

Becoming more mobile in a Hot Wheels wheelchair might seem like a dream come true, but today, Gelato has even more reasons to celebrate: Heâs found his forever home.

It has been revealed that gelato arrived at Cincinnati Animal CARE in Ohio as a stray kitten with a lower-back injury that left him unable to use his hind legs normally. The shelter team wanted to help him move around, but there was a rather inconvenient problem. The wheelchairs they had available were too big for his tiny body.

Now, anyone who has lived with a kitten knows that, besides being irresistibly cute, they can be remarkably determined little creatures. They want to explore everything, investigate every corner, and get involved in whatever their humans are doing. Being unable to move around easily can limit those everyday experiences for the tiny fur balls.

Fortunately, Gelato had people in his corner who weren't about to let his small size stop him from exploring the big world.

Recent findings suggest that the shelter's lead veterinary technician, Mallory Smith, came up with a wonderfully resourceful solution. She built a miniature wheelchair using cardboard, tape, zip ties, wooden rulers, and Hot Wheels toy cars. The first version needed adjustments, but Mallory kept working until the little device was ready to support Gelato as he moved around. While this is certainly quite a unique solution, what isnât unusual is the compassion and creativity behind it. Gelatoâs improvised mobility device is a perfect example of how animal medical care personnel go above and beyond to help patients in need.

Gelato's homemade wheelchair was a clever solution to an immediate problem. However, a makeshift device is not necessarily the best long-term option for a growing kitten with mobility challenges.

Help arrived in the form of an engineer who created a custom 3D-printed wheelchair designed to fit his body and accommodate his growth. The toy cars were gone, but Gelatoâs future mobility was looking more stable.

It has been revealed that gelato got lucky the moment someone refused to give up and asked, "How can we make this work?" This first lucky chance opened him to upcoming opportunities from a wider effort to help one small animal have a better chance at life. Itâs impressive how sometimes sharing an animal's story can make all the difference. A social media post can connect shelters with people who have the skills, resources, or homes that animals need.

Sources indicate that giving Gelato a way to move around was an vital first step. And there was another milestone waiting for him: a loving family of his own.

As the story of Gelatoâs unusual mode of transport spread, drawing plenty of social media attention, it also caught the eye of Hope Hollandsworth, a 28-year-old tattoo artist and devoted cat parent. When she first saw a photograph of Gelato during the summer, she felt immediately drawn to him.

Hollandsworth already cared for two cats with spinal injuries, Bread Crumb and Sprinkles. Both have limited use of their hind legs and rely on their front legs for mobility. She understood that caring for cats with special needs could involve extra responsibilities, adjustments, and plenty of patience.

It has been revealed that in other words, she wasn't going into this adoption without knowing that life with a disabled cat can look a little different. Cat lovers are abundant, but those experienced in caring for disabled felines? Not quite as plentiful.

In a recent development, hope wasted no time, adopting Gelato as soon as she met him at the shelter. The five-month-old kitten spent his first night in his latest home sleeping in her arms.

Absolutely. A disability does not automatically mean that a cat has a poor quality of life. Cats with mobility challenges can still enjoy affection, play, exploration, food puzzles, comfortable naps, and the tech giant of people they trust.

What really matters is understanding the individual cat's needs and making reasonable adjustments to help them live comfortably.

For a cat with a spinal injury, this may include providing easy access to food, water, resting areas, and litter boxes. Non-slip flooring, ramps, and thoughtfully arranged furniture can also help some cats move around more safely. Depending on the injury, a cat may need help with bladder or bowel function, regular skin checks, or a rehabilitation blueprint.

These are not small details. Some cats with spinal injuries cannot empty their bladders normally, which can lead to serious complications without very devoted care. A veterinarian can assess bladder function, mobility, sensation, and other concerns, then explain what support the cat will need at home. The real challenge is finding someone with the time and patience to take over these responsibilities on a daily basis.

Hollandsworth's experience with Bread Crumb and Sprinkles gave her a head start.

According to recent reports, gelato will continue receiving therapy in the hope that he may regain some use of his hind legs, but for now, his recovery is uncertain. Spinal injuries vary, and a cat's prognosis depends on several factors, including the extent of the damage and the neurological function that remains.

But Gelato doesn't need a guaranteed recovery to deserve a happy future. He's got somewhere to go, someone to cuddle, and absolutely no need to prove that he can walk to earn his place in the family.

His newly introduced family is ready to love and support him, whether or not he ever walks on his own. Hollandsworth put it beautifully: to her, Gelato is already perfect just the way he is.

There is a lot of wisdom in that simple sentiment. We can hope for progress, celebrate small improvements, and pursue appropriate treatment without making an animal's worth depend on how much they recover. Loving others, whether animals, people, or even ourselves, for who they are, exactly as they are, is what we call true love.

#216471. Industry News: My Husband Wants To Bring His Girlfriend To Thanksgiving. I’m Not Sure I’m Ready.

Industry News: My Husband Wants To Bring His Girlfriend To Thanksgiving. I’m Not Sure I’m Ready.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just because we have an open relationship doesn’t mean I’m ready for such a substantial step.
  • In a recent development, welcome to Ask A MWLTF (Yes, that’s Mother Who Likes to F*ck.), a monthly anonymous advice column from Scary Mommy.
  • Industry observers note that my husband and I have been open for about two years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just because we have an open relationship doesn’t mean I’m ready for such a substantial step.

In a recent development, welcome to Ask A MWLTF (Yes, that’s Mother Who Likes to F*ck.), a monthly anonymous advice column from Scary Mommy. Here we’ll dissect all your burning questions about motherhood, sex, romance, intimacy, and friendship with the help of our columnist, Penelope, a writer and mental health practitioner in training. She’ll dish out her most sound advice for parents on the delicate dance of raising kids without sacrificing other key relationships. Email her at askpenelope@scarymommy.com.

Industry observers note that my husband and I have been open for about two years. It was something we discussed carefully, and, for the most part, it has worked for us. We have rules, we communicate, and I’ve met a couple of the women he’s dated. I’m not interested in knowing every detail, but I also don’t feel threatened by the fact that he has relationships outside our marriage.

Now he’s been seeing someone for about six months, and he wants to bring her to Thanksgiving at my parents’ house.

In a recent development, we have two kids, and Thanksgiving is a big family holiday for us. My parents, siblings, nieces and nephews will all be there. My husband indicates he wants to stop treating this relationship like something that has to be kept separate from the rest of his life. He says he’s serious about her and thinks including her would make things feel more natural and less secretive.

I understand that. But I also feel strangely territorial. Thanksgiving is one of the few days of the year when I get to be with my whole family, and I don’t particularly want to spend it navigating my husband’s girlfriend. I’m worried about what my parents will think, what the kids will make of it, and whether I’ll spend the entire day feeling like I’m auditioning for the role of Cool, Secure Wife.

Industry observers note that I don’t want to be controlling or make him feel ashamed of a relationship that I’ve agreed he can have. But I also don’t want to be pushed into a level of openness I haven’t agreed to. Am I being unreasonable?

Signed, Not Ready to Pass the Gravy.

It's easy for pressure to arise in a consensually non-monogamous relationship, and it often wears the very respectable outfit of personal growth. You have agreed to be open-minded, so shouldn’t you be open? You have agreed that your husband can love or desire other people, so shouldn’t you be comfortable meeting them? And if you’re not comfortable, does that mean you’re secretly jealous, insecure, or not as evolved as you thought you were?

No. It means you are a person with boundaries, and boundaries do not disappear just because you have made an unconventional relationship choice.

One of the more persistent misunderstandings about non-monogamy is that consent to one arrangement somehow implies consent to all the arrangements that might follow from it. But agreeing that your husband can date other people is not the same as agreeing that those people will become part of your family life. Being comfortable with his girlfriend existing is not the same as wanting her seated next to your Aunt Carol while everyone argues about the turkey.

These are different levels of intimacy. They involve different audiences, different risks, and different emotional demands. You can be genuinely supportive of your husband’s relationship and still want to keep Thanksgiving to the people who have traditionally been part of Thanksgiving.

In fact, I wonder if what you’re reacting to is not simply the presence of another woman, but the feeling that a boundary you thought was understood is being moved. Until now, your husband’s outside relationships have occupied a particular space in your marriage. They may be meaningful, even serious, but they have not been woven into the rituals that organize your family life. Bringing his girlfriend to Thanksgiving would change that. It would make the relationship visible to your parents and children, and it would ask you to participate in presenting it as part of the family.

According to recent reports, that is a significant request. It deserves more than a casual, “Wouldn’t it be nice if she came?”.

Your husband may have a legitimate desire to stop compartmentalizing. He may feel that keeping his girlfriend separate from his family life makes her seem less crucial, or that the secrecy itself is beginning to feel uncomfortable. Those feelings are worth taking seriously. But his desire for integration does not automatically create an obligation for you to provide it, particularly on a holiday that belongs to your family history as much as it belongs to your marriage.

And let’s talk about the children. There is nothing inherently harmful about children knowing that a parent has a romantic relationship with someone other than their spouse. But introducing a partner into family life is not a neutral logistical decision. It raises questions about what the children understand, what they have been told, what they might repeat to relatives, and whether the adults have a shared explanation. If your husband wants his girlfriend to be part of family gatherings, the two of you need to agree on what that means before you put a upcoming person in the middle of a holiday and hope everyone figures it out over pie.

Recent findings suggest that I would also encourage you to resist the temptation to make this a referendum on how good you are at non-monogamy. You do not have to prove your security by accepting every proposed next step. Sometimes the most honest thing you can say is, “I’m okay with your relationship, but I’m not ready for it to occupy this particular space in my life.”.

Sources indicate that that is not a punishment. It is information.

It has been revealed that you might tell your husband something like: “I understand why you want the people in your life to know one another, and I’m not asking you to hide or minimize this relationship. But Thanksgiving with my family feels like too big a first step. I need us to talk about what integrating our relationships into family life would look like, and I don’t want to make that decision under pressure or on a holiday.”.

Then get specific. Does he want you to meet her in a lower-stakes setting first? Does he imagine that she will attend future family events? Does he want the children to know about the relationship? What does she want? Is she comfortable being introduced to your parents as your husband’s girlfriend? And what happens if you discover that you like her, but still don’t want to share Thanksgiving with her? Or if you don’t like her? Or if your husband expects you to be warm and welcoming in a way that feels emotionally dishonest?

These are not small details. They are the actual relationship you’re negotiating.

Recent findings suggest that there is another possibility worth considering: Your husband may be asking for something that sounds like inclusion but is, at least in part, a request for reassurance. Perhaps he wants to know that you accept his girlfriend, that he doesn’t have to split his life into separate compartments, that his happiness won’t always be experienced as a threat to your marriage. If so, you can offer reassurance without agreeing to this particular blueprint. You can say, “I don’t want you to feel ashamed of this relationship. I just don’t want to make Thanksgiving the place where we figure out how to live with it.”.

Recent findings suggest that and if he insists that your reluctance means you aren’t truly comfortable with non-monogamy, I would push back. A relationship agreement is not a blank check. It is an ongoing negotiation, and the terms can become more complicated as people’s feelings and circumstances change. You are allowed to discover that something you thought you could handle feels different when it moves from the abstract to the dining room.

Recent findings suggest that I suspect there is also a useful distinction here between privacy and secrecy. Your husband may be ready to stop keeping his girlfriend a secret. That does not mean every person in his life needs to meet her, or that every family ritual needs to become an opportunity to demonstrate how modern and accepting everyone can be. Privacy is not necessarily shame. Some relationships are simply not ready for the Thanksgiving table.

So perhaps the question isn’t whether his girlfriend gets to come to Thanksgiving this year. It’s whether the two of you can talk about the future of your family life without either of you treating the other’s feelings as evidence of a moral failing. He should be able to tell you that he wants more integration. You should be able to tell him that you’re not ready. Neither of you gets to turn your preference into the only enlightened position.

Recent findings suggest that and for what it’s worth, Thanksgiving is already a holiday with enough emotional labor, complicated family dynamics, and people pretending to enjoy casseroles they hate. You are not obligated to add a major relationship milestone to the menu.

In a recent development, you can take this one holiday at a time. The turkey will survive.
