The kind of ornament that starts a tradition and gets passed down eventually! — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

We have had so much fun with our mini photo printer from Canon — and it's a perfect thing to get before the holidays get rolling. I love taking pictures during a party or event and then handing out hard copies as our guests go out the door. It's such a good, simple party favor. You can also set up homemade photo booths! — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

Do yourself a favor TODAY and buy this Slice tool for cutting wrapping paper. I swear it saved me 7-10 business days while wrapping. I literally hide it from the rest of my family. And while you're at it, buy the Slice box cutter, too. They both make my life easier and happier. — Sarah Aswell.

Before the turkey is steaming on your holiday table... before you need to chop one thousand vegetables for the party, run every knife in your kitchen through this electric knife sharpener. I bring this baby out right before the holidays start and sharpen everything that isn't nailed down in my kitchen, and it almost feels like self-care. Using a sharp knife makes so much more of a difference than you think! — Sarah Aswell.

This is what I've been looking for! I love having cafe lights strung up around my porch for entertaining during the summer — what if they could just MAGICALLY turn into holiday lights for Halloween and then Christmas? Now they can. These programmable lights mean that I am not constantly putting up and taking down lights — the colors just change with the season, in whatever configuration you'd like. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, nothing gets me and my house in the holiday mood quite like having a few really nice candles ready to go. I stay away from the sweeter smells of Christmas and gravitate for ones like this: evergreen and forest smells that are bright and crisp and cheery (even if you opt for a fake tree for your house). — Sarah Aswell.

This combines so many of my interests: puzzles, national parks, and advent calendars! I love that this one involves an activity and that it doesn't result in a bunch of cheap junk in your house that never leaves. — Sarah Aswell.

I love holiday cards, but actually writing them and addressing the envelopes can start to feel like too much of a task, especially with all the other stuff going on around the holidays. I love putting all of my cards, stamps, pens, and stickers in this little case and carrying it with me — I can get a few cards done wherever I am, whether it's my kid's ballet lessons, a doctor's waiting room, or a lunch alone. — Sarah Aswell.

I am really trying to focus my holiday season around activities and togetherness over material things. One great way to do this is to get a few new board games that are super family-friendly. I love this one because it is still playable for kids on the younger side, but it's fun for adults, too. It's also just really pretty and magical and fun — you create lovely worlds with cool animals, for points of course. — Sarah Aswell.

My favorite this season is this dress by Body by Miraclesuit in dark green. You can literally just throw it on and run out the door, and yet it looks so pretty and flattering. And like any good holiday dress, you can elevate it really easily with some heels and jewelry or dress it down with a cardigan and flats. — Sarah Aswell.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hydrangeas really have their moment during the summer months, and then spend the winter looking dead, brown, and crispy while we politely look away. Shea McGee, however, has made a point of doing the opposite, and to beautiful effect!

Industry observers note that that's right, folks; not only did the Netflix Dream Home Makeover star give her hydrangeas some attention in winter, but she also added them to the star of the show during the holidays: her Christmas tree! And, much like Sarah Jessica Parker's floral Christmas tree, it's one of those oh-so-simple but oh-so-effective ideas that we can't believe we didn't think of first.

In a recent development, as you may or may not know, Shea grows Limelight hydrangeas at her Salt Lake City home, telling fans that the blooms “bring me so much joy in the summer”. Is it any wonder, then, that when the interior designer shared a video of her Christmas decor to Instagram, the blooms were front and center?

It has been revealed that A post shared by McGee & Co. (@mcgeeandco).

As you can see above, Shea McGee has decorated her tree with warm brown, tan, and cream ornaments, dried orange slices, clip-on LED candlesticks, and dried hydrangeas from her own garden (although you can buy ready-to-go cone hydrangeas from McGee & Co if you prefer an easier life).

Recent findings suggest that it's a beyond brilliant idea, as it means the blooms get a second act, which is a better return than most shrubs give you. If you want a similar look, just read on for some tips from the experts.

Shop Shea McGee-Inspired Christmas Decor:.

Sources indicate that keen to give it a whirl from scratch? Look this way...

In a recent development, cameron of DreamHowYouLive favors Limelight (the same as Shea McGee grows) and Annabelle for a hydrangea arrangement. “Their petals dry stiff and papery, so they keep their shape, where softer mopheads crumble.”.

In a recent development, flower farmer-florist Joey McFarland of Flowers by Dr. Jo agrees that panicle types like Limelight are best for long stems. He warns that bigleaf hydrangeas set buds in fall, so cutting too deeply means “cutting off your blooms for next year.” Shopping for plants? Browse our list of panicle hydrangea varieties.

It has been revealed that timing is highly important as well, especially when it comes to hydrangeas. Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home waits until the heads “turn papery and antique in early fall.” Cut too soon and, as Cameron warns, “they wilt instead of drying.” (Which means you need to show patience, grasshopper).

When it comes to drying hydrangeas the experts all have a different opinion, which tells you how difficult it can actually be. Floral preservation artist Nadi Melam of Florals Memories states, “I always dry hydrangeas in a vase of water,” about an inch, for a “lovely muted antique color.”.

Cameron hangs them upside down in a dark, dry spot for two or three weeks, since vase-dried heads “tend to droop.” Our guide to drying hydrangea flowers covers both.

It has been revealed that the best rule to follow if you want the Shea McGee effect? Water-drying holds shape and color well, while air-drying is quicker but leaves blooms more fragile.

According to recent reports, there’s one place where most people go wrong when drying hydrangeas for Shea McGee-style decor. As Cameron tells me me he cuts the head town to 3-inch stems, wires each branch and tucks the whole bloom into a gap. His personal rule: “Three small clusters spread around the tree look intentional. One big bunch at the top looks like a mistake.”.

Industry observers note that arslan Ali of DecoroDea advises, “Treat them like picks, not ornaments,” and claims to place them last, “after the ornaments and lights are already on,” so you fill the gaps that are actually still dark. Brooks wires clusters low near the trunk first, then moves smaller heads toward the tips. In essence, you can take a bit from every expert tip.

It has been revealed that for McGee’s look, add dried orange slices, cream and tan ornaments, and warm white lights. Bright white, Cameron notes, makes “the whole thing look cold.”.

Industry observers note that I could go on all day about the importance of a high-quality diet for your cat. But today, I want to talk about an aspect of the feline diet most owners might not think about: the importance of small, consistent, proportioned meals.

Cats evolved as hunters of relatively small prey, so their natural feeding pattern is quite different from ours and from the typical pet dog.

A wild cat might spend much of its day moving through its territory, hunting, and eating multiple small meals when the opportunity presents itself. They are not accustomed to sitting down to one or two large meals each day.

Although the process of domestication means that your feline family member no longer needs to hunt down their next meal, those instincts haven't completely disappeared just because their food comes in a bowl.

Even more so than eating habits, drinking habits in cats are highly tied to their instincts and physiological needs.

It has been revealed that domestic cats evolved from desert wild cats. That arid climate impacted their relationship to water in two key ways:.

First, desert wild cats evolved to get most of their water from their preyâwhich isnât much. This means their kidneys are highly specialized to retain water and pass very little of it through their urine. For a cat that eats several juicy mice each day, this is all well and good. For a pet cat eating dry food, the need to consume water is dramatically increased if they are to keep this super-efficient system running properly. However, the instinct to actively seek out drinking water has not entirely caught up with the domesticated catâs lifestyle.

Sources indicate that this brings us to cat hydration key number two: Desert wild cats know better than to drink stagnant water. In hot, arid climates, still water breeds bacteria and other dangerous organisms. As a result, cats are naturally attracted to fresh, flowing water that is much safer to drink; something that remains true for our pets.

Your kitty may be a skilled hunter and the apex predator of your home, but, like their wildcat ancestors, they can also be prey animals, with instincts that evolved to evade larger predators. One place this becomes evident is in their bathroom habits.

Cats bury their urine and feces to hide the scent from potential predators and competitors, so a stinky litter box feels anything but safe. And if they donât feel safe there, they may find other places to eliminate waste. Or worse, hold it in, causing kidney and digestive concerns.

Industry observers note that A quiet place to rest, a predictable routine, and the freedom to explore without being pushed can help a dog settle in. Rewarding small steps with positive reinforcement builds confidence without turning every new experience into a test.

Sources indicate that adjusting to a new life takes time, and there's no need to rush it. A dog who hides under the table on day one isn't a failed adoption. A dog who isn't ready for cuddles isn't being ungrateful. Theyâre figuring things out, and they need time to decide that this strange new place might actually be safe. Building trust and confidence can be a slow process.

According to recent reports, those familiar with the process of adopting or fostering dogs, particularly those who may not have had the best start to life, may have heard of the 3-3-3 Rule for Dogs: 3 days, 3 weeks, 3 months. Itâs a simplified interpretation of the timeline many dogs tend to follow when adjusting to a fresh home environment.

The first 3 days are about decompression and resetting the nervous system. It might look like a dog that is timid, constantly moving, hiding, or even showing signs of aggression. In a recent development, my cat, Mitzi, is 16 years and 8 months old. She has early-stage kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, which she is on medication for. About 2 months ago, she became deaf, and since then has refused to leave the master bedroom. I have moved her water bowl and litter box there and feed her there.

Is there anything I can do to get her to come out?â.

At her age, sweet Mitzi has certainly earned the right to enjoy her golden years at her own pace, but I can imagine it is difficult to see her withdraw from the rest of the house, especially when you remember how she used to move around. However, I would not necessarily interpret her reluctance to leave the bedroom as something we need to correct. Losing her hearing can be quite disorienting. Imagine walking into a room where you can no longer hear footsteps, familiar voices, or the little sounds that help you understand what is happening around you. For Mitzi, the bedroom may now feel like her safest little world, where everything is familiar and predictable.

According to recent reports, I actually think you have done a wonderful job adapting her environment by bringing her food, water, and litter box closer. Rather than encouraging her to leave right away, I would focus on helping her feel confident enough to explore if she wishes. You could start by sitting with her near the bedroom doorway, offering a favorite treat or a little affection. Gradually place treats a short distance beyond the door, allowing her to decide whether she wants to investigate.

Take care to only approach her within her visual field, avoid startling her while she sleeps, and keep pathways clear and nonslip. Think of it as extending her upcoming world one comfortable step at a time, rather than asking her to return to her old routine.

According to recent reports, there is one thing I would not overlook, though. Mitzi has both chronic kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, and at her age, reduced mobility or withdrawal can also be associated with arthritis, high blood pressure, visual changes, or inadequate control of her thyroid disease. I would recommend a senior cat veterinary checkup that includes blood pressure measurement, assessment for arthritis, and follow-up kidney and thyroid testing. Sometimes what looks like a behavioral change is actually a senior cat quietly telling us that they are in pain and something does not feel quite right.

Most importantly, please do not feel that you are encouraging a bad habit by keeping her essentials in the bedroom. You are adapting her home to meet her changing needs, and that is a beautiful expression of your love and care for her. If the bedroom is where Mitzi feels safe, eats well, drinks, uses her litter box, and enjoys your company, that can be a perfectly good quality of life.

At this stage, happiness is not measured by how much of the house she explores, but by how comfortable and secure she feels in the little world she chooses.

What Your Snake Plant Needs in November – 5 Winter Care Checks to Keep It Glossy and Thriving

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say.
  • Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right.
  • It has been revealed that take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most of the year, a snake plant really is about as hard to kill as people say. But that changes in November. The days get short, and the heat comes on, and the watering habit you kept all summer now leaves the potting mix wet for weeks. Yellow leaves and soft, mushy bases tend to follow.

Good snake plant care in winter is mostly about doing less and getting the timing right. Once light levels drop, your snake plant isn't growing much, so it uses far less water and needs no fertilizer at all. What it does need is a dry pot between drinks, steady room temperatures, and a spot out of the cold air that pools along windows.

It has been revealed that take a few minutes with your plant in front of you and work through five checks. Run through them now, then again on a gray afternoon in December. That alone considerably cuts the odds of losing a snake plant to winter.

Don't rely on a calendar when watering snake plants. A snake plant that needed water every two weeks in July might go a month or more between drinks in November. Its surface won't tell you much. So how do you know when it's dry? Push a finger down as far as it goes, or try the chopstick trick: push a wooden skewer to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. Damp mix clings to the wood and darkens it; dry mix leaves it clean.

If you're struggling to know when to water, then use a moisture meter for an accurate assessment, like the Xlux instant read probe, available from Amazon. Water only when the whole depth comes up dry, then let the pot drain fully. Leaves that go soft or flop over at the soil line usually mean the roots have sat wet too long.

According to recent reports, low light is something a snake plant tolerates, not something it grows well in. In November, the sun sits lower and the days are short, so a dim corner that was fine in June may now get very little light. Growth slows, and the mix stays wet far longer because the plant is barely drawing water.

It has been revealed that A spot within a few feet (about a meter) of an east or west window helps. Make the move gradual, though – a plant that goes straight from a dim hallway into hours of direct south sun can scorch.

Without a bright window, a grow light like the Sansi Pot-Clip-On Grow Light, positioned a foot or so (30 cm) above the leaves, fills the gap.

On a cold evening, hold the back of your hand near the window where your snake plant sits. Chilly on your skin means chilly on the leaves, too. Blame single-pane glass, the gap under an outside door, or a nearby heating vent. Any of them can swing the temperature more than a snake plant can take – even while the thermostat reads fine.

According to recent reports, ordinary room temperatures are what you're after, roughly 60–85°F (16–29°C). Trouble starts if the plant sits below about 50°F (10°C) for long stretches. Leaves pressed against cold glass can develop soft, water-soaked patches. So at night, pull the pot back a foot or two (30–60cm) from the window.

If you want to see what the plant goes through after dark, then use a high/low thermometer, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer, which displays both high and low temperature and humidity levels.

Sources indicate that tip the pot and look underneath. Drainage holes get plugged with compacted mix, a stray pebble, or roots that have grown through. In a decorative cachepot, a snake plant can stand in an inch (2.5 cm) of old water without anyone noticing. Lift it out and check. If the mix is still wet a week or more after you watered, it may have broken down and is holding too much moisture.

Winter is a poor time to disturb roots, so repotting snake plants is normally a spring job. The exception is a pot that won't drain at all – or a mix that stays soggy no matter what. Then a careful repot now beats rotting roots in March. For a replacement, choose a pot with a drainage hole and its own saucer, like this Vigoro ceramic planter from Home Depot. Fill it with a gritty potting mix, like Miracle-Gro Cactus, Palm, and Citrus Mix, which drains much faster than regular potting soil.

It has been revealed that look each leaf over, down to the soil line, for signs of common snake plant problems. If yellow is creeping up from the base and the leaf feels soft or mushy there, you're looking at overwatering and rotting roots. Cold damage can look a lot like it, though. Wrinkled or curling leaves usually mean the reverse: the plant went too long between drinks.

In a recent development, next, check the crevices where leaves overlap for pests. Cottony white tufts there are mealybugs (Planococcus citri), and small tan or brown bumps that stay put when nudged are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

Sources indicate that dab a few with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, then follow up with a ready-to-use insecticidal soap, like Garden Safe insecticidal soap, sprayed right onto the insects. It's far easier to deal with a dozen now than hundreds in February.

Put the fertilizer away until spring. A plant that isn't actively growing can't use the feed, so unused salts build up in the mix and can burn roots. Hold off on routine repotting for the same reason. Fresh mix and a bigger pot push a plant toward newly introduced growth right when the light to support it is lowest. Disturbed roots also recover slowly in a cool room.

According to recent reports, don't water your snake plant on a schedule just because the heat is drying out the air. Dry air and dry soil aren't the same thing, and a snake plant copes with dry air far better than it does with wet roots. For the next few months, you want it holding steady, not growing.

Run the same five checks again around the latest year. In winter, a snake plant mostly needs the right spot and to be left alone. Give it that, and the one looking a bit tired in November is usually putting up new leaves by late spring.

Dogs have been a fixture of family life for thousands of years, and many people who grew up with one say they canât picture their childhood without them. Beyond the obvious benefits of companionship and fun, growing up with a dog has been shown to have positive effects on physical and emotional well-being; advantages that show up in how children handle friendships, feelings, and everyday challenges.

Of course, this doesnât mean that having a dog is right for everyone. Bringing a dog into your home is a big decision that affects budgets and daily routines for years to come, and the best outcomes tend to come from families who go in with open eyes.

For anyone considering life with a dog, here are a few ways they can improve a childâs life, and things to consider before adopting one.

Growing up around animals can lower the chance of developing allergies later on. Dogs, and all the things that come with living with them, expose children to a range of allergens, which helps build a more robust immune system. The key seems to be early exposure, which means the sooner a dog becomes part of a childâs world, the better.

Children who are close to their dogs tend to be more securely attached to their parents, and theyâre more likely to form strong friendships, too. Strong relationships in one part of a childâs life seem to go hand in hand with strong relationships in others. Kids who share more physical contact with their dogs, from cuddles to roughhousing, tend to get along better with their moms, dads, and friends.

Kids who grow up with a family dog tend to have lower rates of anxiety. The benefits reach well beyond childhood, too. Dogs can ease feelings of depression and anxiety in adults who went through childhood trauma, and they can reduce signs of post-traumatic stress, which is part of the reason theyâre so often brought into therapy.

A dog is a living, breathing creature with needs, and children who help care for one learn responsibility and dependability. A five-year-old canât take on every chore, but age-appropriate tasks are a great place to start. Young children spend much of their lives at the mercy of parents and teachers, so having a dog to look after can give them a real sense of empowerment and build self-esteem.

In a recent development, caring for an animal from an early age also builds empathy, which supports emotional intelligence and helps a child grow into a more compassionate person. The lessons go on from there. Dogs model loyalty; training and bonding teach patience, and learning to read a dogâs body language and respect their boundaries teaches respect. When a family pet eventually passes away, children also learn about death and grieving.

According to recent reports, children with pets tend to have better self-esteem than children without them. The effect appears to be strongest as kids approach adolescence; an age when the emotional support of a companion animal may matter most.

It has been revealed that families with dogs tend to be more physically active than their peers, getting about 11 extra minutes of exercise a day. That may not sound like much, but it adds up to roughly 5.5 hours a month in a society that is growing more sedentary all the time.

For some children, the effect is far larger. Girls in particular gained around 52 minutes of light physical activity a day after a dog joined the family. The flip side was striking too, since girls who lost their pet saw their daily activity drop by 62 minutes.

Children tend to handle stressful moments better with a dog nearby. They feel happier and more at ease, and being able to touch the dog calms them even further. Simply having a furry companion close by seems to help kids feel steadier inside.

For all the upsides, adopting a dog isnât a decision to take lightly, and there are a few things every family needs to consider before racing out to get a four-legged friend.

Budget: Dogs depend on their owners for food, veterinary care, and emergencies, and a household budget that canât cover those costs is a reason to rethink the strategy.

Age: Although many childhood benefits increase the earlier they start living with a dog, sometimes waiting until children are older is a good idea. St. Bernards make fantastic family pets, for example, but they can weigh as much as 180 pounds and can hurt a child accidentally. Small breeds have their own risks, since they can be fragile and prone to injury until kids learn boundaries and how to respect animals.

Lifestyle: A family that works long hours and spends every evening shuttling children to activities needs a plan for what the dog will be doing. Not every schedule has room for a pet, and that is perfectly fine, but a dog shouldnât be adopted without free time to spend with it.

Motivation: Children often beg for a dog, promising to walk, feed, and pick up after them.

In a recent development, then, the novelty fades, and the adults end up with the bulk of the care. Although itâs a good idea to encourage children to take on some of the responsibility of looking after a dog, you should assume that youâll be the one doing most of the work â hope for the best, strategy for the worst!

Growing up alongside a dog can bring real benefits, from fewer allergies and lower anxiety to stronger relationships and more time spent moving. But to enjoy the benefits of living with a dog, families need to have the time, money, and genuine desire to take care of one.

Growing up with a dog might not guarantee health and happiness, but itâs a pretty good place to start!

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

Raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. Cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

In a recent development, unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very swiftly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. According to recent reports, rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so vital.

Industry observers note that when people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

According to recent reports, in cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. As the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

According to recent reports, there is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. According to recent reports, here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

And remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

If your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

According to recent reports, keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

If a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

And please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

In a recent development, long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

Stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in Upcoming Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

In a recent development, when the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

Recent findings suggest that after surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

Stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

During the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

Conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

Stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a new generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

In a recent development, stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

Recent findings suggest that every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

It has been revealed that support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

In a recent development, learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

In a recent development, keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Industry observers note that follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

In a recent development, these dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

In a recent development, if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Recent findings suggest that the holidays often leave us with more food than we know what to do with, don't they? Before throwing everything into the compost or bin, though, take a look at your Thanksgiving leftovers; your feathered friends could be very thankful for them!

Yes, some everyday ingredients from the feasting table can make welcome treats for backyard birds, offering a little extra nourishment as temperatures drop and the nights draw in (and transform your outdoor space into a welcoming bird sanctuary in the process).

Whether you're hoping to see your birth month bird out there, or just happy to offer your kitchen scraps up to any local critters who might make use of them, here's how to use your Thanksgiving leftovers to keep bird feeders filled over the holidays...

Before we dive on in, a word of caution: not every Thanksgiving dish is suitable for wildlife, especially as salt, butter, rich sauces and seasonings can make seemingly harmless scraps unsuitable for birds.

According to recent reports, the trick? Try to save a few simple ingredients before they make their way into the casserole dish or onto the dinner table. With that caveat in place, then, here are seven Thanksgiving kitchen scraps worth keeping...

In a recent development, have a few apples left over from your Thanksgiving preparations? Birds such as robins and other fruit-eating visitors will definitely appreciate small pieces of fresh apple.

Cut the flesh into bite-sized chunks, removing the core and seeds first. Bruised apples are fine so long as they're fresh (they're not as fussy as we are!), but discard any mouldy or spoiled pieces. And avoid offering apple pie filling or cooked apples covered in sugar and spices.

It has been revealed that cranberries are a Thanksgiving staple, and you'd better believe that their fresh (and unseasoned, obviously) counterparts make a lovely treat for birds. Offer a few whole or chopped cranberries on a clean feeding tray like this one from MIXXIDEA.

Recent findings suggest that frozen cranberries are fine, too, once thawed. Just avoid cranberry sauce, as it typically contains added sugar and may include other ingredients birds don't need. Honestly, a little fresh fruit is all that's required.

In a recent development, pecans (again, plain and unsalted) are another holiday favorite that can be shared with feathered visitors, along with walnuts and peanuts. All of these scrummy nuts are rife at Thanksgiving, and all provide fats and protein that can help birds maintain their energy during colder weather.

Take care to chop larger nuts into manageable pieces and check that they haven't been coated in salt, sugar, chocolate or seasoning. Just like the fruit, nuts should be fresh, too, rather than stale or musty.

Corn often features on the Thanksgiving menu in a big way, and a few plain kernels can be offered to garden birds; just set aside a small portion before adding butter, salt or other seasonings.

Cooked or fresh corn kernels can be placed on a feeding tray, but avoid creamed corn, buttery corn casserole and heavily seasoned dishes. Only offer a little at a time, as damp corn can spoil promptly.

If pumpkin or squash features in your holiday cooking (or your Thanksgiving decor, if you're Kristin Davis!), don't throw away all those seeds; instead, rinse away any stringy pulp, remove any seasoning and allow the seeds to dry thoroughly.

Sources indicate that offer them (have I gotten too repetitive yet?) plain and unsalted, either whole for larger birds or broken into smaller pieces for smaller visitors. They're a useful source of fats and nutrients, making them a worthwhile addition to your bird feeding station.

It has been revealed that leftover rice can also be shared with birds from your Thanksgiving feast, provided it hasn't been cooked with salt, butter, oil, garlic or onions. Both white and brown rice are suitable in small quantities when prepared plainly.

Industry observers note that P.S. There's a persistent myth that uncooked or cooked rice swells inside birds and causes harm, but this isn't true. Nevertheless, rice shouldn't replace more nutritious bird food, so just offer just a small amount (you may find your birth month winter bird adores it) and remove anything uneaten so it doesn't have a chance to go bad.

A little leftover boiled or baked potato from your Thanksgiving prep can be another treat for your feathered friends. Set aside a portion before adding butter, milk, salt or gravy, then allow it to cool and chop it into small pieces.

In a recent development, please never offer raw potatoes or green potato peelings, and avoid chips, roast potatoes cooked in fat and heavily seasoned mashed potatoes. Experts always advise that plain potato be treated as an occasional extra rather than a regular food source.

It's every bit as notable to know what to avoid when it comes to feeding birds your Thanksgiving leftovers. Turkey fat and pan drippings might seem like an easy substitute for bird suet, but they're best kept off the feeding station. Audubon, in fact, warns that turkey fat melts more readily than traditional suet and can turn rancid quickly. It can also smear onto feathers, potentially affecting their waterproofing and insulation.

Industry observers note that gravy, stuffing and salty side dishes should also stay off the menu, as they often contain butter, salt, onion and garlic, none of which are suitable additions to a wild bird's diet. Avoid, too, anything that contains chocolate, along with avocado, sugary desserts and heavily processed foods, too. Bread and pastry aren't particularly nutritious (even if they won't do any harm), so think up some better ways to use your leftovers; might this author humbly submit the idea of a bread-and-butter pudding?

In a recent development, once you've picked all of the bird-friendly scraps out of your Thanksgiving feast, be sure to present it properly! Always use a clean feeding tray rather than leaving piles of food on the ground, and try to put food out in the morning, as this is when it's most likely to be eaten.

Take care to remove anything uneaten before it spoils, and wash feeding surfaces regularly to reduce the risk of bacteria and disease spreading. It's also worth keeping fresh drinking water available, particularly as colder weather approaches, and remember that kitchen scraps are supposed to be occasional extras, not a replacement for a balanced wild bird food mix.

Still, all those warnings aside, there's no denying that sharing a little of your holiday feast with your local birds is a lovely way to give thanks to Mother Nature (and reduce food waste at the same time).

The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Lowering the risk: Genetics play a big part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Industry observers note that kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which highlights up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

Industry observers note that feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

Sources indicate that lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

Industry observers note that this is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight quickly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

In a recent development, up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

Industry observers note that lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

Lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

Sources indicate that feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Recent findings suggest that lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a plan for each cat.

It has been revealed that I have a question about my dog, Jethro. Sometimes when he alerts, the hackles between his shoulders rise. Other times they are prominent along his lower back. What does each appearance indicate about how he is responding?â.

That is a great observation! When a dogâs hackles rise, it is an involuntary response controlled by the autonomic nervous system called piloerection, and it tells us that his arousal level has increased. However, the location of the raised hair does not reliably tell us which emotion a dog is experiencing.

When the hackles rise between his shoulders, it can accompany alertness, excitement, uncertainty, or concern. When they appear along his lower back, the same range of emotional responses is possible. Neither pattern automatically indicates aggression, fear, or a particular level of threat. Think of hackles as a little emotional alarm bell; they tell us Jethro is experiencing heightened arousal, but not exactly why.

Recent findings suggest that different dogs will respond to different stimuli in different ways, so thereâs no âone size fits allâ explanation for why different areas are triggered. I would pay close attention to what is happening around him when this occurs. Is he alerting to a stranger approaching the house, another dog walking past, an unfamiliar noise, or something unexpected in the environment? You might want to start keeping a record of what is going on before and after Jethroâs hackles are raised, and whether itâs his shoulders or lower back that is involved.

According to recent reports, combine that context with his facial expression, ear position, tail carriage, posture, muscle tension, and ability to disengage. Looking at the whole picture helps us understand whether Jethro is curious, excited, uncertain, or uncomfortable, and, most importantly, how we can best support him. These details, together with what triggered the alert, give us a much clearer picture of how Jethro is feeling.

Your Compost Pile Needs These 6 Things Before Winter If You Want to Make Black Gold Through the Cold

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Did you know that your compost pile keeps working over winter?
  • According to recent reports, during winter composting, microorganisms slow down their activities, and freezing temperatures can temporarily stop them, but they won’t necessarily die.
  • It has been revealed that tackle these six tasks now to keep composting at home this winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Did you know that your compost pile keeps working over winter? While the decomposition process might slow, microorganisms are still active in compost as long as it doesn’t freeze. Ignoring your compost over winter is a missed opportunity to keep making and using the garden's black gold.

According to recent reports, during winter composting, microorganisms slow down their activities, and freezing temperatures can temporarily stop them, but they won’t necessarily die. A sufficiently large and well-managed compost pile can stay warm enough in the center to keep the little critters working and breaking down waste materials.

It has been revealed that tackle these six tasks now to keep composting at home this winter. Even if decomposition slows in the cold, these steps will help you get more usable compost earlier next spring. Our tips work for all main types of composting, including open heaps, compost bins, and enclosed tumblers.

Now is a good time to remove any finished compost to use as winter mulch in your garden beds. Then, it’s time for one last turn for the season. Turning compost helps aerate the pile, introducing oxygen to the microorganisms that need it to decompose materials. It also distributes moisture and materials more evenly.

A sturdy garden fork will do the job, but a compost aerator tool, like this Squeeze Master one from Amazon, makes it much easier to get air deep into the pile without having to dig everything out and turn it by hand.

Recent findings suggest that this should be your final turn before freezing conditions begin. You don’t want to keep turning compost over the winter, as this will release heat and slow the decomposition process. As you make the final turn, look for and break up any wet clumps or large pieces of material that haven’t broken down much. If you note a sour or rotten smell, add more dry, brown materials.

Recent findings suggest that larger compost piles retain heat better than smaller piles because they have a greater volume of material relative to their surface area, which is exposed to the cold. The more you can add to your pile now, the more likely it is that the center will remain warm and active throughout winter. A long-probe compost thermometer, like the Vivosun Compost, is a handy way to check what's happening deep inside the pile without disturbing it.

For a compost pile, aim for three feet (0.9 m) wide, deep, and high. Bulk up your pile during your final turn, adding a good mix of green and brown materials. Be sure to add enough dry, coarse material to absorb moisture. A large pile won’t be any good if it becomes waterlogged and so compacted that there is no airflow.

While you don’t want to turn your compost again this winter, you can still add layers of waste to it as the season progresses. Green materials, like kitchen scraps, keep coming all winter, but brown materials tend to be harder to come by. Browns include dry leaves and twigs as well as cardboard, untreated paper, and straw.

In a recent development, good compost should have layers of each type of material, so stockpile your harder-to-find browns now. As you add kitchen scraps over the winter, layer in some of these stockpiled brown materials to maintain a good balance. A countertop compost caddy, like the Oxo Good Grips Easy-Clean Compost Bin, makes it easy to collect kitchen waste indoors until you're ready to take it outside. Keep a bin or pile of leaves and twigs from fall yard waste, as well as shredded paper and cardboard.

According to recent reports, A large pile with extra waste material will help insulate the active center of your compost pile, but you can also take extra steps to insulate and protect it from cold winter temperatures. This will slow heat loss. It’s crucial that you take insulating steps before the compost pile freezes.

One easy way to insulate the pile is to surround it on all sides with straw bales or bags of leaves. If you don't have straw on hand, you can pick up full-sized straw bales from Tractor Supply to create a protective barrier around your compost pile. You can also add a layer of straw or leaves on top. Wood chips and finished compost are also efficient insulators.

Industry observers note that if you have a bin or tumbler, another option is to surround it with insulating materials. Just be sure you still have easy access to add materials throughout winter.

Sources indicate that winter precipitation can saturate a compost pile, causing it to become compacted and reducing airflow. Moisture can also wash away the valuable nutrients you’re trying to collect. If you have an open compost pile, cover it with a tarp that will allow precipitation to run off and away from the compost. A heavy-duty Everbilt tarp from Home Depot is a durable option that you can secure in place to keep winter rain and snow out. If you have a bin, keep a lid on it.

While keeping moisture out is important, compost still needs airflow in winter. Don’t completely seal your pile with protective coverings. If you have a bin with a cover, there should be drainage and air holes. Make sure these don’t get clogged.

In a recent development, moisture balance is always key in compost. It’s important to check and adjust this balance before your compost freezes this winter. To optimize microorganism activity, the composting material should feel damp when you squeeze it in your hand without excess moisture running out of it.

If your compost feels too wet, incorporate more dry, brown material. If the pile is too dry, you can add a little water before there is a real danger of it freezing. Throughout winter, as long as temperatures allow it, continue to check the pile for moisture balance and adjust as needed.

Industry observers note that many gardeners might wonder: are these efforts worthwhile, or does compost just shut down for winter? Compost does continue to break down in winter, sometimes with temporary stops during freezing conditions.

It has been revealed that however, it’s crucial to have realistic expectations. While microorganisms continue to break down compostable materials in winter, their processes do slow down significantly. Larger, insulated piles are more likely to stay active and break down faster than smaller piles or compost in uninsulated bins. Taking these steps to keep your pile warmer in winter is worth the effort if you can keep microorganisms active and working.

It’s crucial to note that if you practice vermicomposting, you should provide extra protection for the worms over winter. To keep it active over winter, keep your vermicompost bin indoors where you can control the temperature.

Industry observers note that winter doesn't have to put composting on hold. A little preparation in autumn can protect valuable organic material, reduce household waste, and give you a head start on producing nutrient-rich compost for the next growing season.

Puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

According to recent reports, the opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Puppies learn rapidly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

Industry observers note that all puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

It has been revealed that food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Recent findings suggest that obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and newly introduced situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health concerns is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

In a recent development, most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

In a recent development, researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

Activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

According to recent reports, A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health issues. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

Did you know that your catâs skin accounts for about a quarter of their body weight? With that in mind, it should be no surprise that your catâs skin uses an incredible amount of the nutrients they consume, especially protein. In fact, fur is composed of approximately 95% protein, and hair growth and skin renewal can account for roughly 25 to 30% of daily protein requirements.1 Dietary fats are equally important, as essential fatty acids help maintain the skinâs protective barrier and support a soft, supple coat.

Because of this, if your cat isnât getting enough protein, omega fatty acids, and other essential nutrients in their diet, it is often the skin that reveals the first signs. A dull, brittle coat, excessive shedding, flaky skin, or hair loss may signal nutritional deficiencies.

The larger problem? Many cat foods on the market donât provide enough protein to meet the needs of the skin and coat, as well as the rest of their body. And even fewer foods provide enough quality fatty acids.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, New York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Sources indicate that chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Recent findings suggest that chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, promptly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the manufacturer commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

In a recent development, in 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

According to recent reports, in January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

Sources indicate that chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Sources indicate that every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

In a recent development, follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

Recent findings suggest that these dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair. Many of us willingly put ourselves through torturous procedures to remove it from our legs, armpits, and just about anywhere else, while, at the same time, the quest to keep a full and lustrous head of hair fuels a billion-dollar hair growth industry. Since the 1980s, a chemical called Minoxidil has become increasingly popular as both a topical and oral treatment for baldness, but what few people realize is that the very product promising hair growth poses a serious risk to their pets. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) is warning consumers about minoxidil toxicity in cats and dogs, highlighting a danger that deserves considerably more attention.

Anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule. Cats rub against our heads, groom our hair, curl up on our pillows, and somehow manage to investigate just about everything we touch. These perfectly normal feline behaviors can turn deadly when minoxidil enters the picture.

The history of minoxidil shares similarities with another well-known human drug: Viagra, which essentially took a common side effect of the heart medication, sildenafil, and turned it into its primary purpose. In the 1970s, researchers developing a new blood pressure medication found that a common side effect of the drug, minoxidil, was hypertrichosis, aka excessive hair growth. Like the story of sildenafil, the makers of minoxidil leaned into this side effect, repurposing the drug as a treatment for hair loss.1.

Sources indicate that in 1988, the FDA officially approved minoxidil, and it quickly gained popularity in products like Rogaine. Minoxidil works by widening blood vessels, a process called vasodilation, and altering the hair growth cycle to stimulate hair growth. But what helps us fight hair loss can be dangerous for our feline roommates.

Sources indicate that A 2021 study published in the Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association examined 211 reported cases of topical minoxidil exposure in dogs and cats. Of the 87 animals that developed signs of poisoning, 62 were cats, and 25 were dogs. Eight cats died. A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology identified another 94 reported cases, including 68 cats, ten of which died. Notably, 55 of 57 cases involving accidental exposure to a person's minoxidil treatment involved cats.

How does this happen? Topical minoxidil is applied directly to the scalp, either as a liquid using a dropper or as a foam spread with the fingers. Medication can remain on the hands, hair, or nearby surfaces. Cats don't need to break into the medicine cabinet; a little grooming, an affectionate head rub, or a snooze on a contaminated pillow may be enough to expose them. Some were even exposed through everyday contact with their follicle-challenged cat parents.

Industry observers note that minoxidil works by relaxing blood vessels and improving blood flow. In cats, however, the effects can become dangerously disruptive.

According to recent reports, when absorbed, it can cause blood pressure to drop dramatically, a condition called hypotension. To compensate, the heart beats faster, but this doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Serious complications can follow, including fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema) or in the space surrounding them (pleural effusion). Breathing becomes increasingly difficult, and severe poisoning can progress to cardiovascular and respiratory failure.

Now, what should you look out for? You might notice unusual tiredness, weakness, vomiting, or a sudden loss of appetite. More concerningly, your kitty may start breathing faster than usual or appear to struggle for air. And here's the tricky part: some cats may initially seem perfectly fine.

That's why a suspected exposure should never be brushed off simply because your cat appears normal. Waiting for visible signs of poisoning can waste valuable time.

Now that we are beginning to appreciate the risks this product poses to our pets, we have to wonder how many unexplained cat and dog deaths could be attributed to unknown minoxidil exposure.

Rapunzel may have had a tower to keep her hair safe, but cat owners need a different strategy: keeping minoxidil well away from curious paws.

If you use topical minoxidil, make sure you apply it in a room your cat cannot access. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water immediately afterward, and clean up any spills promptly. Used tissues, cotton pads, applicators, and empty containers should go straight into a secure bin. That tissue you casually leave on the bathroom counter? To your cat, it might look like just another interesting thing to investigate.

Sources indicate that and what about bedtime? If you apply minoxidil in your bedroom, make closing the door part of your nighttime routine. Your cat may protest being left out of the bedroom, especially if your pillow is their favorite sleeping spot, but keeping them away from treated hair, skin, pillows, and bedding can help prevent accidental contact with medication residue. Remember, allowing the product to dry does not guarantee that every surface is free from contamination.

Recent findings suggest that you might be wondering whether switching to oral minoxidil would solve the problem. Unfortunately, not entirely. Oral minoxidil is also toxic to cats if they accidentally ingest a tablet. Whichever formulation you use, keep the medication securely stored and well out of paws' reach. Or better yet, look into options that donât put your pet at risk.

According to recent reports, discuss your household's furry residents with the prescribing dermatologist and establish a routine that prevents accidental exposure. Cats are wonderfully persistent creatures. They may not appreciate a closed door or understand why their favorite pillow is suddenly off-limits, but a little inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping them safe.

If your cat licks minoxidil, contacts a spill, or may have groomed contaminated fur, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control service immediately, even if your kitty seems perfectly fine.

According to recent reports, treatment depends on the exposure and your cat's condition. It may involve hospitalization, cardiovascular monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous support, and medications to manage complications such as low blood pressure or fluid accumulation.

Never attempt to induce vomiting or administer home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinary professional. If medication is still on your cat's coat or skin, ask your veterinarian how to handle decontamination safely rather than delaying emergency care.

Unfortunately, not every cat survives minoxidil poisoning, making every accidental exposure a veterinary emergency.
