In a recent development, working on the floor strains your back, while working on dining tables risks costly dents and scratches. Instead, it’s always good to have a portable workbench that’s easy to set up and take down, like the Keter Folding Workbench. A stable and reliable surface makes projects more efficient, since you won’t need to be bending over to cut, glue, or drill.

Sources indicate that additionally, the workbench can act as a simple support when you need to measure materials, set up a miter saw, or clamp your materials so that they don’t shift while you work. If you don’t want to purchase or build a newly introduced workbench for this purpose, you can also set up a pair of heavy-duty collapsible sawhorses paired with a sacrificial plywood sheet to give you a waist-high surface that folds flat for storage.

Industry observers note that floor and countertop protection prevents permanent damage and can reduce your cleanup time by half. For this reason, it’s essential to plan for surface protection and cleanup when you are setting up your temporary workshop.

Drape moving blankets or thick canvas drop cloths over tables, counters, or hardwood floors to absorb impacts and catch dropped tools. Unlike plastic tarps, heavy canvas stays put and prevents items from sliding around. To help keep your temporary workshop clean and organized, include a small wet/dry shop vac fitted with a disposable fleece filter bag to capture messes at the source so you can pack up in minutes.

Treated with a special coating, this heavy-duty tarp repels moisture in addition to offering protection to your work surface. Learn more.

Without a heavy, bolted-down bench vise, clamps act as your third hand to hold materials steady while cutting, gluing, or drilling. Keep two or three medium-sized bar clamps handy to secure materials directly to a table edge or sawhorse. These clamps are often easy to store when not in use, so they won’t get in the way while you work.

In a recent development, also, you can lay a rubberized mesh pad, like this POWERTEC Nonslip Mat, under smaller pieces when sanding or routing. It holds flat workpieces steady using friction alone, leaving the entire top surface unobstructed.

It has been revealed that overhead room lighting casts shadows right over your hands when you lean over a project to see what you are doing, increasing mistakes and safety risks. But holding a flashlight while you work just ties up one of your hands, severely limiting your control and efficiency. Instead, it’s better to find task lights that are made for versatility so you can focus on the project, rather than fighting with dim lighting.

A directional light clipped to a shelf, chair, or table edge lets you aim bright light directly at your cut line or assembly area. Opt for a high-lumen LED clamp light or magnetic work light to illuminate your temporary workshop, like this ZONE LED Clamp Work Light.

Sources indicate that indoor outlets are often far from where you need to work and rarely have enough open receptacles. A 12-gauge, multi-outlet cord with built-in GFCI protection, such as this CCCEI Extension Cord, safely handles high-draw power tools while protecting you from electrical faults. Industry observers note that use a thick-gauge cord to safely run high-draw power tools from a wall outlet to your temporary station without overheating or losing power. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

Industry observers note that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s key to solidify your shoveling plan before the first snow flies.

It has been revealed that “Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”.

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

Shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” indicates grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

To make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” says Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”.

According to recent reports, A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” says Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”.

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aliaksandr Bahdanovich/Getty Images.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” indicates Flores.

Industry observers note that the fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, says Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, claims Lopez.

Just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

“Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” states Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”.

A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

In a recent development, “Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” claims Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

After a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

It has been revealed that pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” states Lopez. “.

Recent findings suggest that try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

It has been revealed that “Before winter arrives, strategy where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” notes Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”.

Also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

It has been revealed that aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

It has been revealed that safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” says Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural issue.”.

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

To stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” says Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”.

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” says Schwab.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

“Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” indicates Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”.

Industry observers note that obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

Recent findings suggest that start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” states Flores.

Homeowners with boxelder trees (a type of maple tree that produces seed-bearing pods) may be all too familiar with the bugs that tend to follow. Boxelder bugs, named for their preferred host, are ½-inch-long black insects with red or orange markings along their wings. They feed on seeds and leaves from boxelders and a few other trees like ash and maple, but they don’t cause serious damage to plants, homes, or humans. Still, when these bugs gather in large numbers, they become a major nuisance—especially when they invade homes and release their distinctive, musty smell.

Industry observers note that in fall, boxelder bugs migrate toward warmth, often swarming on the south- and west-facing walls of homes, garages, sheds, and trees. If they find small cracks or gaps, they’ll slip inside to overwinter in walls, attics, or basements—sometimes appearing indoors on sunny winter days. Even homes without box elder trees nearby aren’t entirely safe: These bugs are highly attracted to warmth and light-colored siding, making them a common seasonal pest in many regions.

If you’re tired of seeing these bugs on your siding—or worse, inside your house—take charge now with these smart strategies for getting rid of boxelder bugs.

Boxelder bugs (Boisea trivittata) are easy to recognize once you know what to look for. Adult bugs are about ½ inch long, with black bodies and reddish-orange markings along their wings and thorax. Their long, oval shape and bold color contrast make them easy to spot—especially when they gather in large groups on sunny walls or trees.

Sources indicate that juvenile boxelder bugs, known as nymphs, are smaller and bright red with no wings, though they develop darker coloration and wing pads as they mature. You’ll typically see these bugs in late summer and fall, when both adults and nymphs are most active.

Sources indicate that despite their intimidating appearance, boxelder bugs are harmless to people, pets, and homes. They don’t bite or sting, and they won’t eat through drywall, wood, or furniture. However, their tendency to swarm in large numbers—and release a pungent odor when crushed—makes them a frustrating nuisance pest, especially when they get indoors.

Boxelder bugs are often mistaken for other insects, like stink bugs or milkweed bugs. What sets them apart is their distinctive red-lined wings, flattened body, and preference for warm, sunlit surfaces. If you notice clusters of bugs on the south or west sides of your home, windows, or trees in fall, you’re likely dealing with boxelder bugs.

In a recent development, boxelder bugs follow a predictable seasonal pattern, which explains why they seem to appear all at once. In spring, adults emerge from their overwintering spots—usually inside walls or attics—and head outdoors to feed and lay eggs on box elder, maple, and ash trees.

According to recent reports, by summer, the eggs hatch into bright red nymphs, which mature into winged adults by late summer. These adults become most visible in fall, when they gather in large numbers on sunlit walls and tree trunks, especially on the south and west sides of homes.

As temperatures drop, they look for cracks and gaps in buildings to overwinter indoors. Though mostly dormant through winter, they may occasionally reappear on warm, sunny days—often near windows or light sources.

Knowing their seasonal behavior makes it easier to time prevention efforts, especially in early fall when they begin looking for a way inside.

If the bugs are in your house, don’t panic—they won’t bite, sting, or reproduce inside. Still, their smell and stains can be unpleasant. Use these simple methods to get them out and keep them from coming back.

Boxelder bugs slip in through small cracks around windows, doors, vents, and siding.

Do this in early fall before they try to move in for winter. Once they’re inside, they’re much harder to control.

In a recent development, boxelder bugs often hide in basements, attics, or ceiling corners, especially during colder months. To catch the sneaky ones, set up glue or light-based traps in these low-traffic areas.

Recent findings suggest that replace traps regularly to avoid lingering odors. While traps won’t eliminate a boxelder bug infestation, they’re a great supplemental tool for catching stragglers inside the home.

For quick, chemical-free control, just vacuum up any boxelder bugs you find on floors, windowsills, or walls.

Boxelder bugs don’t reproduce indoors. Once you’ve cleared them out and sealed up entry points, they shouldn’t come back.

Instead of reaching for harsh chemical pesticides (they’re not very helpful here), mix up a DIY soap spray to kill boxelder bugs on contact.

In a recent development, boxelder bugs are most active outdoors in late summer and fall, especially around sunny walls, tree trunks, and light-colored siding. Taking action early can reduce the number trying to get indoors.

If you spot small groups of boxelder bugs gathering on your home’s siding, foundation, or trees, a strong blast from a garden hose can break them up.

Reducing their numbers outside can help you avoid a full-blown infestation indoors later on.

For larger swarms, diatomaceous earth is a natural and pet-safe way to kill boxelder bugs outdoors.

According to recent reports, this fine powder pierces the bugs’ exoskeletons, causing them to dry out and die within hours. Reapply diatomaceous earth after it rains, or if the bugs return.

Industry observers note that in general, chemical sprays are not the first recommendation for managing boxelder bugs. Experts at the University of California Integrated Pest Management program advise that insecticide sprays are often no more effective than vacuuming or using a garden hose, and require repeated application for limited results.

However, if bugs are clustered on the exterior of your house and you’ve already tried sealing, trapping, vacuuming, and all of these other recommendations, a professional-grade perimeter spray may help. For persistent infestations in late summer or early fall, a licensed pest professional may apply EPA-approved synthetic pyrethroid insecticides (like deltamethrin, bifenthrin, cyfluthrin, or permethrin) to the foundation, siding seams, eaves, window and door trim, and attic vents to create a residual barrier.

Industry observers note that since the pests feed on the seedpods of female box elder trees, removing them and replacing them with non-seed-bearing male trees (or other species) can help you get rid of the bugs permanently. Keep in mind that the more mature the tree, the costlier it will be to remove. Also, consider that the benefits of the tree—shade, privacy, and curb appeal—may outweigh the insect nuisance.

Warm fall weather and nearby box elder, maple, or ash trees attract the bugs to sunlit walls and cracks.

Remove seed-bearing trees, seal entry points, clean up debris, and use non-chemical control methods.

Electrical tape comes in plenty of colors, but each has a purpose. Here's what the common shades mean in U.S. electrical work.

Being a DIY electrician is one way homeowners like to save a little money over expensive repairs. However, there are safety concerns when it comes to doing your own electrical work. Electrical tape color meanings help electricians identify wires and make sense of connections that might otherwise look identical. The trouble is that colors don’t always mean the same thing.

Learn what the common colors usually mean, how electricians use them, and why a strip of tape can’t confirm a wire’s purpose.

Electricians use colored tape to identify wires, especially when several look alike. In the United States, the colors commonly mean:.

These colors aren’t universal. The National Electrical Code sets rules for identifying neutral and grounding wires, but most hot-wire colors follow common practices rather than strict requirements. For example, orange can have a specific meaning in certain commercial electrical systems. Its purpose depends on the wiring, so electricians can’t rely on color alone.

In a recent development, electricians often wrap colored tape around the ends of wires to tell them apart. Manufacturers such as 3M make tape specifically for identifying different electrical connections.

Tape can also show when a wire serves a different purpose than its original color suggests. For example, electricians may mark a white wire with black tape to identify it as a hot wire in certain situations. Electrical codes limit when and how they can make these changes.

Recent findings suggest that however, tape color alone can’t confirm a wire’s purpose or whether it carries electricity. Previous repairs, incorrect markings, or different labeling practices can cause confusion. Before starting electrical work, a qualified person should identify the circuit and test that the power is off. Homeowners who encounter unfamiliar or conflicting wire markings should have a licensed electrician inspect the wiring.

#216316. "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

"Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'm serializing my fresh Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.
  • Recent findings suggest that throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels.
  • Yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm serializing my fresh Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.

Recent findings suggest that throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels. The first precedent on this was Brandreth v. Lance (1839), an 1839 Newly introduced York trial court decision. This was followed by State ex rel. Liversey v. Judge (1882), an 1882 Louisiana Supreme Court decision. Subsequent decisions helped establish this as a firm rule, seemingly culminating in Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson.

Yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels. By my count the court systems of thirty-four states have either so held or have in practice been so acting, with only six states plus D.C. continuing to categorically bar such injunctions. {See Eugene Volokh, Anti-Libel Injunctions, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 73 (2019).}.

Sources indicate that this trend seems to have accelerated with the rise of the internet. Historically, a libel has been a short, sharp shock—typically, a one-time article in a newspaper that is printed and can't be removed—with the only possible remedy being damages or criminal prosecution. But the internet can turn libel into a steady drip, drip, drip of damage, with more readers seeing a libelous web page every day. Injunctions thus seem a more useful remedy.

The internet also makes it easier for judgment-proof defendants to cause real damage; an injunction can thus be useful in a way that a damages remedy might not be. Criminal libel is theoretically available in about ten states, and there are indeed likely a couple of dozen criminal libel prosecutions in the United States each year. But in most states the only way to deploy criminal remedies in service of protecting reputation is through getting an injunction that can be enforced through the threat of criminal contempt.

It has been revealed that are these injunctions contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment? The answer turns out to be complicated, especially if we focus on permanent injunctions, entered to forbid the repetition of material found to be libelous in a final judgment (with the defendant having had an opportunity to call for a jury trial).

It's true that early sources often view the freedom of the press as precluding prior restraints: To quote William Blackstone, "The liberty of the press is indeed essential to the nature of a free state: but this consists in laying no previous restraints upon publications, and not in freedom from censure for criminal matter when published." Yet this doesn't quite speak to the modern question whether the law may restrain repetition of material for matter found to be criminal (or tortious).

It has been revealed that nor does it speak to whether the law may require removal of such matter after a trial: Removal just wasn't practically an option in the print era. In such situations of injunctions against repetition of an already published libel or ordering its removal, "[e]very freeman" would retain the "undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases before the public" (again quoting Blackstone) at least in the first instance.

Nor is there a "restrictive power of a licenser" or "control of an inspector" in the sense that the Framers likely understood licensers, which is to say officials administering a licensing system. (To quote St. George Tucker, under that system "all books printed were previously licensed by some of the great offices of state, or the two universities, and all foreign books were exposed to a similar scrutiny before they were vended.") The injunction is imposed by a judge, often following a jury verdict, administering justice between two parties, not running a traditional licensing system that "subject[s] all freedom of sentiment to the prejudices of one man, and make[s] him the arbitrary and infallible judge of all controverted points in learning, religion, and government.".

Likewise, early sources stressed the importance of allowing a jury to resolve what is true and false in libel cases. But, as I noted, the modern permanent injunction in libel cases is entered after a final judgment on the merits, which at least in principle allows a defendant to demand a jury trial. If the defendant has so demanded, then any injunction would be based on the jury verdict.

It has been revealed that this stems in part from the twentieth-century merger of law and equity, since equitable remedies, such as injunctions, can now be issued following the use of the legal procedure of a jury trial. (Historically, one argument against injunctions in libel cases has been that "equity will not enjoin a libel," a statement about the limits of the equity courts more than about constitutional protections for free expression.) Indeed, the Delaware Court of Chancery, which operates in a state system where law and equity remain largely separate, has continued to hold that it generally can't enjoin libel. But it expressly left open the possibility that, once the Delaware Superior Court (the law court) concludes—after a jury trial, if the parties don't choose a bench trial—that a statement is libelous, an injunction can then be issued.

Sources indicate that in practice, anti-libel injunctions are often parts of default judgments, or follow bench trials, and thus don't involve factual findings by juries. In both those situations, though, the defendant can be said to have waived his right to a jury trial. To be sure, temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are entered before any opportunity for a jury trial—but for that reason many courts continue to reject them on First Amendment grounds.

And, as the California Supreme Court held in allowing such post-final-judgment permanent injunctions, the reasoning of Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson expressly sets aside injunctions in traditional civil libel disputes:.

Industry observers note that the high court was careful to point out … that the statute being considered was "not aimed at the redress of individual or private wrongs. Remedies for libel remain available and unaffected." … But most significant is that the court … clarified that it was not addressing "questions as to the extent of authority to prevent publications in order to protect private rights according to the principles governing the exercise of the jurisdiction of courts of equity." In a footnote, the court cited [an] … article by Roscoe Pound that observed that English courts permit "an injunction in case the libel was repeated or publication was continued after a jury had found the matter libelous." Therefore, Near expressly did not address the issue posed in the present case.

The Supreme Court hasn't confronted such permanent injunctions against repetition of proven libel since Near, but it has authorized injunctions against obscenity (which Near had anticipated) and against commercial speech that proposes illegal transactions. The one case in which it granted certiorari as to anti-libel injunctions, Tory v. Cochran (2005), largely disappeared when the plaintiff, famed lawyer Johnnie Cochran, died while the case was pending. None of these cases discussed the original meaning of the First Amendment, and the lower court cases dealing with the matter have largely not discussed it, either.

So here we have a fairly rich body of originalist evidence related to libel law generally. We have a considerable body of evidence from before and shortly after the Framing that talks about "previous restraints." And we have some nineteenth-century sources that seem to take the view that all injunctions in libel cases are unconstitutional. But how exactly do the Framing-era sources apply to a permanent anti-libel injunction issued by a court following the resolution of a libel case? Hard to know for sure.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors. Here's why cities give them out and what recipients actually receive.

Whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause. But what does the key actually do?

Cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize. Learn what a key to the city represents, how the custom began, and what someone actually gets to do with it.

A key to the city is an award that cities give to people they want to honor.

“The Key to the City is presented as a symbol of civic recognition and Philadelphia’s appreciation for individuals whose achievements, service and influence have made a meaningful impact on the city and its people,” according to a release from the City of Philadelphia.

The key is usually decorative, with the city’s name or seal on it. Some come in a display box or with a certificate. Little Rock, Arkansas, considers its key the city’s highest ceremonial honor.

But the key won’t open City Hall or any other public building. It doesn’t give the recipient special privileges or any authority, either. In 2010, New York City tried something different with an art project that gave people working keys to certain locations. Those weren’t the same as the city’s usual honorary keys.

Industry observers note that the tradition goes back to when cities had walls and gates that closed at night. Giving someone a key meant they could come and go without asking permission.

It has been revealed that in medieval Europe, leaders also exchanged keys during official visits or military surrenders. Handing over the keys sometimes meant giving up control of a city. Over time, the custom became a way to welcome or honor someone.

Today, cities give keys to athletes, public figures, volunteers, and local residents. Each city has its own rules for who receives one.

It has been revealed that philadelphia, for example, honored a resident in 2026 after he walked across the country to support career opportunities for young people. Elk Grove, California, recognizes military accomplishments and acts of heroism, while Little Rock reserves its keys for people who live outside Arkansas.

Industry observers note that mayors usually present the keys, although some cities involve the city council or accept nominations from residents. Recipients get a keepsake and some public recognition, but no special privileges.

Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent New York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):.

The motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of New York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

Recent findings suggest that on September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the New York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine.".

Respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

Industry observers note that among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also said that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

Industry observers note that at his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

He also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

According to recent reports, the parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

Recent findings suggest that the record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical concerns at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

Industry observers note that under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

Industry observers note that respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.

“The metal wheels of a refrigerator can scratch, dent or gouge just about any flooring surface. Laying down stiff cardboard or a piece of leftover carpet provides an effective barrier, but for the best protection, use a sheet of 1/8‑in. hardboard. The smooth surface protects floors and helps appliances slide into and out of place. —ANTHONY LOMBARDI.

Sources indicate that “To find out if power outages ruined the food in your freezer while you were away on vacation, freeze a container of water and rest a penny on top of the ice. If the penny is at the bottom when you get back, it means the power was off long enough to melt the water—as well as thaw (and likely spoil) everything in the freezer. —JOHN NAKAMURA.

Dan Roberts for Family Handyman.

“If you don’t have a label handy, use a rubber band instead. Stretch it around your Mason jar, then write the contents with a permanent marker. The grippy rubber also makes the jar easier to open. —DAVID KOWALCZYK Picture Frame Message Board I wanted a nicer-looking place for my weekly grocery list and family notes, so I turned a picture frame into a dry-erase board. I simply cut decorative paper to fit the frame and put it behind the glass, creating a surface I can write on with a dryerase marker. —JESSIE DAWSON.

Sources indicate that “For a minor scorch mark on a laminate countertop, skip the abrasive cleaner. Buff it out with car wax or a mixture of toothpaste and baking soda instead.” —ELAINE WHITFIELD.

“Leaky seals around faucets and sink rims can lead to slow but severe damage (they can destroy a countertop, for example). So after installing a newly introduced sink or faucet, dribble water around the area and wait a few minutes. Then get under the sink and look for leaks. —GREGORY PRITCHARD.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes it’s tough to mix foods such as old-fashioned oily peanut butter in a small jar by hand. But if you enjoy reaching for a power tool to solve a problem as I do, head out to the garage. As it turns out, the handle of a mixing spoon fits perfectly in the chuck of a cordless drill. —CLIFF MERCER.

Recent findings suggest that “Build a simple dispenser for your trash bags using 1/2-in. pipe and a few fittings. Screw a floor flange to the cabinet, thread in a 3-in.-long pipe nipple, and then thread a 90-degree elbow onto the nipple. Cut the vertical pipe so it’s a bit longer than the width of the roll of bags. Finally, thread the vertical piece into the elbow and slip on the roll.” —TRAVIS LARSON.

Recent findings suggest that “I turn sandwich-size bags into snack-size bags by heating up an old butter knife with a lighter and slicing the bag in half. The hot knife cauterizes the edges of the two newly introduced bags, and the cauterized edges are just as strong as the factory-sealed edges.” —JULIA TRENTON.

“Need to sharpen a utility knife, pocket blade or scissors but don’t have a sharpening stone on hand? Flip a ceramic mug and use the unglazed ring on the bottom as a sharpener. Hold the blade at a 45-degree angle and slide it across the ring in one direction, from the base to the tip. This won’t replace a proper sharpening kit, but it can rapidly clean up a dull edge in a pinch.” —RONALD ALVAREZ.

According to recent reports, “Ice packs are a great way to keep your lunch cool, but they can be expensive to replace if you tend to lose them. To make your own reusable version without spending a lot, soak a sponge in water, then place it in a small resealable plastic bag. Freeze it overnight, then pop it into your lunch container. As the ice melts, the bag holds the water until the sponge reabsorbs it. When you get home, simply refreeze the pack for next time. I like to keep several on hand to use in lunches and coolers, as well as for first aid. They’re inexpensive to make, easy to reuse and help reduce waste.” —TOM SHERIDAN.

Emiko Franzen for Family Handyman.

Recent findings suggest that “Alphabetizing spices helps you swiftly find what your recipe calls for and makes putting away jars just as fast. Another benefit? You can easily figure out which spices are missing from your pantry, so you’re less likely to discover you’re out of a key ingredient halfway through making a meal. Take a quick glance before grocery shopping to keep staples stocked.” —MARTIN SUTHERLAND.

Recent findings suggest that “When your favorite candle burns too low for a lighter or match to reach the wick, don’t risk burning your fingertips. Instead, light a piece of uncooked spaghetti. It is long enough to reach deep into tall candle holders and burns long enough to light the wick.” —PATRICIA HART.

“For an extra-fresh garbage disposal, toss in a few lemon or lime peels. Run the disposal with cold water until you can’t hear any more grinding, then run it for another 30 seconds (with the water still on).” —GREGORY HOLT.

According to recent reports, “A countertop isn’t the best place to keep a recipe while you’re cooking. It takes up counter space, is difficult to read and is bound to get splattered. Instead, use a clothes hanger with pants clips to hang the recipe from a cabinet handle. Open the book or magazine to the desired page (or use a printout), clamp it in place and you have a simple hanging stand. This trick works best with smaller cookbooks, magazines or single-sheet recipes.” —GLENN WHITE.

“My kitchen drawers used to be an absolute wreck, with pans and dishes crammed in however they’d fit. And seemingly every time I needed something, it was at the very bottom of the drawer. My solution was to cut a piece of 1/8-in. pegboard to the size of the drawer bottom and attach dowels using screws from underneath. Now my pans are organized and easy to access. The 10 minutes it took to build was easily made up with how much frustration it has saved me.” —JIM DAVIDSON.

According to recent reports, “Crawling under a kitchen sink to refill the soap dispenser was a hassle, so I tried filling it from above. But when I did, the soap formed an air-lock bubble and overflowed, creating a mess. That’s when I came up with the idea of inserting a drinking straw in the dispenser neck to relieve “bubble block.” Now when I refill the dispenser, the air escapes through the straw and the soap stays where it belongs.” —PAUL SNYDER.

In a recent development, “A dishwasher makes quick work of disinfecting washable toys such as plastic building blocks. Drop the blocks in a mesh laundry bag and run your dishwasher as usual. Remove the bag before the drying cycle, letting the blocks air-dry on a towel. This method also works for items such as seashells, dish brushes, sponges and rags.” —ROBERT VALENTI.

Industry observers note that “If your refrigerator stops dispensing water after you change the filter, make sure the new filter is fully seated. Many people don’t twist it in completely, and one final turn may be all it takes to get the dispenser working again.” —STANLEY BEAUMONT.

It has been revealed that “An ironing board with the cover removed can be used as an extra cooling rack when you’re doing a lot of baking. Better yet, it frees up valuable counter space for other kitchen tasks. Just be sure to use pans, paper liners, parchment or some other barrier between baked goods and the board.” —LIZ GRABOWSKI.

Katie Synold for Family Handyman.

It has been revealed that “When the rubber sink baffle on my garbage disposal gets grimy or starts to smell, I switch off the power at the breaker and scrub it with an old toothbrush dipped in hot, soapy water and baking soda. I lift the rubber flaps to clean underneath, where food and grime collect. Then I restore power, rinse it with cold water and run the disposal briefly to flush away the debris.” —CHARLES MCALLISTER.

To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

It has been revealed that after selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

Industry observers note that the best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

Recent findings suggest that countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

According to recent reports, reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Big Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

Faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

Industry observers note that two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more important to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

Most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

Sources indicate that many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

Recent findings suggest that then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

Capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

According to recent reports, flow rate—how quickly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another vital consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

Industry observers note that every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

Recent findings suggest that water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

It has been revealed that no, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

Most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Sources indicate that filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need new filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • On May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others.
  • Industry observers note that these appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that from the 4-judge unsigned majority opinion in Patterson v. Meta Platforms, Inc., decided today by N.Y.'s high court:.

On May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others. Plaintiffs, victims of the shooting and their family members, commenced these actions against the shooter's parents, firearms manufacturers, and social media companies, seeking compensation for their injuries.

Industry observers note that these appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence. Specifically, plaintiffs contend that their complaints state causes of action for products liability based on defective features of these social media defendants' platforms and their failure to warn thereof….

Industry observers note that [P]laintiffs failed to adequately plead that features of [the] social media defendants' products proximately caused their injuries. Generally, a defendant's acts qualify as a proximate cause when they are "a substantial cause of the events which produced the injury." This inquiry examines.

"the foreseeability of the event resulting in injury; the passage of time between the originally negligent act and the intervening act; the spatial gap, if any, between the original act and the intervening act; whether the original act of negligence was a completed occurrence or was ongoing at the time of the intervening act; whether and, if so, what other forces combined to bring about the harm; as well as public policy considerations regarding the scope of liability.".

Foreseeability is often the most significant factor. Indeed, if an unforeseeable intervening criminal act of a third party causes the plaintiff's injury, the causal connection is severed. Thus, proximate causation will not be found when the intervening act "is extraordinary under the circumstances, not foreseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of or far removed from the defendant's conduct." "Although foreseeability and proximate cause are generally questions for the factfinder, there are instances in which proximate cause can be determined as a matter of law because 'only one conclusion may be drawn from the established facts'" such as when "the original negligent act merely 'furnished the occasion for'—but did not cause—'an unrelated act to cause injuries not ordinarily anticipated.'".

Sources indicate that here, plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the remaining social media defendants' product defects proximately caused the shooter to carry out the mass shooting that resulted in plaintiffs' injuries. The complaints, even accepting the factual allegations as true, fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants' decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.

Sources indicate that instead, under the circumstances, the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. {Our conclusion is limited to the unusual facts of this case, where the platforms' assertedly addictive features were alleged to have harmed the shooter rather than the plaintiffs directly.} We therefore need not address the scope of section 230 of the Communications Decency Act or how it would apply to the claims against these defendants.

Judge Halligan joined the majority, but also wrote a concurring opinion:.

I join the majority because I agree that the plaintiffs have not adequately pleaded proximate causation. I write separately to underscore that, for me, this conclusion rests squarely on the highly unusual facts presented here, and to offer some additional thoughts regarding the scope of section 230.

As an initial matter, I agree with my dissenting colleagues that the plaintiffs alleged that several of the defendants tortiously designed addictive products. The complaints make a number of general claims about social media and youth: that defendants' platforms are addictive; that compulsive use of social media, particularly by young people, causes emotional disturbance and "impulsive decision-making and risk-taking behavior"; and that such use can also yield other deleterious consequences, including "sleep disturbances, mental health problems and suicidal ideation, and violent, hateful acts." The complaints further assert that the social media defendants, knowing of the addictive quality of their products and the heightened susceptibility of young people, not only failed to implement features for limiting use or warning parents, but also took deliberate advantage of that vulnerability by utilizing "strategic timing and clustering of notifications to lure back users" and by implementing "barriers to the deactivation and deletion of accounts." ….

I find the claims before us quite distinct from the cases cited by the dissent that have allowed products liability claims premised on the addictiveness of social media platforms to proceed. I have little doubt that a plaintiff could allege a sufficient connection between the design of a platform and adverse consequences for the mental health of young customers. In those cases, the harms that form the basis for the claims—for example, the alleged inducement of "compulsive use among young users to the detriment of their health and well-being"—flow directly from the platforms' allegedly defective features, leaving little question "that the defective design was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff's injury.".

Sources indicate that but the plaintiffs here are not bringing a claim on behalf of users. Instead, they are seeking recompense for the victims of a crime committed by a social media user. In other words, the allegedly addictive properties of the platforms were not alleged to have harmed the plaintiffs here directly, but rather to have harmed the shooter, who in turn engaged in extensive research and planning before murdering ten people and wounding others…. I do not see the connection between the two as sufficiently articulated to allow the case to proceed.

Industry observers note that three aspects of these claims inform my conclusion. First, although intervening criminal acts do not necessarily sever the causal chain, the shooter's conduct was apparently painstakingly planned and extraordinarily violent.

It has been revealed that second, the prominence of content in many of plaintiffs' allegations gives me real pause. Even if we were to interpret section 230 as not immunizing defendants against claims for actions that rest, at least in part, on content, I am not aware of other instances where a court has held that provocative content proximately caused someone to commit a violent crime, and I am hesitant to take that step here. {I understand the plaintiffs to disclaim on appeal any effort to base liability on defendants' roles as publishers of content. But their complaints can be read to allege that the platforms are defective at least in part because of the racist and extremist content they make available, and the plaintiffs acknowledge that content is a necessary link in the causal chain leading to their harms.}.

Third, the defendants' platforms have billions of worldwide owners. To the extent that proximate cause could rest on a correlation between social media use and a specific type of harmful act committed by any one of those users, the potential liability would sweep broadly, to say the least. If all such conduct were "a natural and foreseeable consequence" of a platform's design choices, the concept of proximate cause would have little meaning….

Sources indicate that as for section 230, …. "we [have] read section 230 to bar 'lawsuits seeking to hold a service provider liable for its exercise of a publisher's traditional editorial functions.'" … Our endorsement of a "traditional editorial functions" test for section 230 immunity, however, does little to answer whether the conduct of modern social media platforms can be labelled such a function.

As to claims that a defendant designed its platform features to encourage or facilitate addiction, irrespective of the particular content promoted by the platform, I agree with the dissent that they are not barred by section 230. That is because such conduct does not constitute a traditional editorial function, even under a broad understanding of that term.

As to claims that challenge a social media platform's use of content-recommendation algorithms, the dissent appears to take the view that content-recommendation algorithms which are designed to be addictive are not covered by section 230 immunity, since they increase engagement in a way that could not have been envisioned at the time that provision was enacted in 1996. I have no quarrel with how we framed the scope of section 230 in Shiamili: the key question is whether a platform engaged in a traditional editorial function, akin to a decision "to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter content." But whether platforms' use of content-recommendation algorithms can be said to resemble traditional decisions to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content is, for me, a more difficult question….

[O]verly broad interpretations of section 230 in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape are unmoored from Congress's purpose in enacting that provision—to protect minors from being exposed to pornography online…. Given that caution, I would not be inclined to extend section 230's reach to all content-recommendation algorithms. I am particularly skeptical that use of individualized content-recommendation algorithms—that is, algorithms that "assess[ ] a user's prior posts, friends, or viewing habits to recommend new content and connections"—constitutes a traditional publisher function. After all, "[t]raditional publication has never included selecting the news, opinion pieces, or classified ads to send to each individual reader based on guesses as to their preferences and interests." Instead, such functions may be "more analogous to the actions of a direct marketer, matchmaker, or recruiter than to those of a publisher.".

In my view, a closer question is presented as to engagement-maximizing algorithms that, unlike the algorithms described above, do not take into account any individual user's conduct but instead seek to "promote[ ] third-party content" based on "cumulative user engagement." On one hand, algorithms that do not respond to individual user conduct may be thought to resemble a publisher's traditional aim of presenting content that owners, on the whole, want to see. On the other hand, one might conclude that "generic" content-based algorithms bear no more resemblance to traditional publication than their "'advanced'—individualized—counterparts" because they still rely on an assessment of user viewing habits in a manner akin to "a direct marketer" rather than a traditional publisher. My dissenting colleagues offer yet another variation on this point; they assert that engagement-maximizing algorithms differ from an editor's choice of where to place a news story because the algorithms are "designed to prey on neurological frailties and alter brain chemistry.".

Whether section 230 protects any of these algorithms is, for me, a difficult question, and I do not think the record before us sheds much light on how different types of content-recommendation algorithms actually operate on the social media defendants' individual platforms—information that might affect my view. We need not decide those questions today because, whatever the scope of the "traditional editorial functions" protected by section 230, the plaintiffs have failed to sufficiently allege that the defendants' platforms' features caused their grave injuries.

Judge Rivera, joined by Chief Judge Wilson and Judge Troutman, dissented in relevant part; an excerpt from the very long opinion:.

It has been revealed that the complaints detail the shooter's transformation from a seemingly ordinary teenager into a virulent racist and violent white supremacist…. [In his manifesto, t]he shooter also wrote that he "was not born racist nor [did he] gr[o]w up to be racist." Rather, he was exposed to and indoctrinated in his ideology of racial violence after using various social media platforms, starting with Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat in his early teen years, before he transitioned to more niche platforms like Reddit, Discord, Twitch and 4chan. The shooter claimed he swiftly "became transfixed with and addicted to [the] online world." He wrote in his diary:.

"I'm addict[ed] to consoooooming. It's 2 in the morning. w[hat] t[he] f[*ck] … I'll admit my mental health has seriously degraded these past few years, especially in the last few months. I should be sleeping right now. I'm just browsing online:/" (emphasis added).

By his own account, he sacrificed "years of [his] life" to being online, often "stay[ing] up late" "browsing Reddit or watching YouTube" "every day." He stated that his compulsive social media use "seriously degraded" his mental health and isolated him from his peers. Rather than "go[ing] to friend's houses" or other social gatherings, "[e]very day after school [he] would just go home and play games and watch YouTube, mostly by [him]self." Ultimately, as he descended further into isolation, he believed he had no other choice but to commit this barbarous act.

Plaintiffs allege that the shooter's experience of compulsive social media engagement is widespread because the products' addictive features are fundamental to the social media defendants' business model. According to plaintiffs, defendants' business models seek to maximize user engagement through products "designed to be addictive." Plaintiffs assert that the operation of these products on the shooter, and their adverse impact on his mind caused by their addictive features, are links in the proximate causal chain underlying plaintiffs' tort liability causes of action against the social media defendants….

In a recent development, the Appellate Division erroneously concluded that defendants are immune from plaintiffs' lawsuit under Section 230. As I discuss, Section 230 does not shield defendants from plaintiffs' products liability and failure to warn allegations grounded on allegedly addictive products, as those claims have nothing to do with defendants' role as a third-party content publisher or as the creator of protected speech….

Sources indicate that to the extent plaintiffs' claims against the social media defendants are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content, including racist, white supremacist, and violent content, defendants are immune from suit pursuant to Section 230. However, not all claims asserted in the complaints are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content. Rather, as I explain, the complaints also stated causes of action based on defendants' design of allegedly defective products and failure to warn….

According to recent reports, plaintiffs assert that these defendants are civilly liable for their role in addicting the shooter to social media and consequent deterioration of his mental health. Plaintiffs' complaints set forth the entire chain of causation that allegedly led to the mass shooting. By designing highly addictive algorithms known to cause severe mental harm to teenagers—like the shooter—the social media defendants created a direct link to the resulting damages, particularly given their failure to warn users and parents of these risks…. [T]here is no Section 230 immunity that attaches to the architecture of defendants' social media products—particularly their purposefully addictive algorithms….

It has been revealed that defendants' alternative argument that the complaints were properly dismissed on First Amendment grounds is unpersuasive. At this pre-answer stage of the litigation, it is unclear how precisely the content-recommendation algorithms function, meaning it is not possible to determine, as a matter of law, on a motion to dismiss that the algorithms themselves are protected speech. That determination requires factual findings dependent on future discovery. On a motion to dismiss we only decide whether the plaintiffs' claim is cognizable and not whether it will eventually succeed based on the facts established by the record….

And here's a short excerpt from the dissent's long discussion of why it rejects the majority's proximate cause theory:.

It has been revealed that the majority's conclusion that plaintiffs "fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence" of the social media defendants' platforms because "the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law" is unsupported by our well-established tort liability doctrines. First, we have made clear that there may be more than one link in a causal chain and there may be more than one tortfeasor liable, jointly or individually, for a plaintiff's injuries. "[T]he mere fact that other persons share some responsibility for [the] plaintiff's harm does not absolve [a] defendant from liability." Thus, the fact that the third-party content creators may bear responsibility for the harm does not mean that defendants bear none.

Second, a defect need only be a "substantial cause"—not the sole cause—"of the events which produced the injury." Substantial means more than slight or trivial. Plaintiffs' allegations that defendants' product adversely affected the shooter's mental health and behavior, making him a compulsive social media user, with the attendant negative impact on his mind and body, isolated from others, rendering him more susceptible to commit this horrific violent act, easily satisfies the "substantial cause" standard.

Sources indicate that third, not all intervening acts break the causal chain. An intervening act only breaks the causal nexus if it is extraordinary under the circumstances, unforeseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of and far removed from the defendant's conduct. That determination depends on whether the intervening act and its consequences were the foreseeable result of a defendant's tortious conduct. Even the "intentional" or "criminal" intervening acts of a third party can be reasonably foreseeable….

[W]hile here, the harm arose from exposure to graphic violence and white supremacist propaganda, plaintiffs allege that the algorithm is content-agnostic. According to plaintiffs, defendants' products and platforms rely on these complex algorithms to keep owners engaged, which negatively impacts young people's mental health, and, in turn, increases the tendency to violent behavior, all the while driving revenue for these defendants. Thus, the majority's assertion that the shooter's actions were not foreseeable is nothing more than a factual conclusion, but that determination cannot be made by the Court on a motion to dismiss….

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a upcoming parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

In a recent development, parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

According to recent reports, diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

Drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

According to recent reports, not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”.

The benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

There’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”.

Back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.
